This research proposes a new method for quality link assessment and data collection management in wireless sensor networks using a decentralized approach.
Initially, the algorithm calculates the communication quality between nodes by analyzing packet transmission errors and uses this information to create a hierarchical cluster system with ranges.
When needed, this algorithm can quickly execute a data collection task by targeting only specific cluster heads, reducing the number of active nodes and the consumption of limited power in sensors.
Simulations show that in comparison to other strategies, this algorithm significantly lowers the number of nodes that must be active during data collection and consumes less power on average.

The field of computer vision can leverage scene context to enhance the performance of deep object detectors, a concept this paper explores from multiple perspectives. It discusses available scene context data sources and proposes a framework for examining how these aspects affect objects and detectors. This is followed by a review of deep learning methods that utilize scene context, a compilation of evaluation metrics used in this area, and suggestions for improving current approaches. The paper concludes by outlining potential research directions for context-aware deep object detection.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate an elliptic system of Kirchhoff type that incorporates a sequence of nonhomogeneous terms and growth restrictions similar to those found in the Trudinger-Moser class. The primary focus is on establishing the compactness of the embedding and obtaining solutions for the given system. We have considered two distinct scenarios in this study: the homogeneous case, the Dirichlet problem, and the non-Dirichlet problem. Additionally, the solution for the given system can be derived from the solutions for the corresponding decoupled equations under specific conditions, thus making several existing results for Kirchhoff type systems more unified and generalized.

We have derived an improved bound for the probability mass of the event occurring when independent random variables, having slightly higher expectations and being logically disconnected, contribute to the occurrence of an event. An analogous result has been established for variables that are logically connected. Our findings lead to better consequences, including an improved bound for the concentration phenomenon of sums of independently distributed variables and estimates for the probabilities related to random matrices and adjacency matrices of weighted graphs.

Let $p$ be an odd prime and $W(k)$ denote the ring of Witt vectors of characteristic $p$ algebraic closure $k$ of $\mathbb{Q}_p$. This paper offers a classification of unramified mixed characteristic $(0,0)$-weights over the ring of power series $W[k]$. A specific, full-rank submodule of the power series ring is identified, with coefficients from $W[k]$, and its elements correspond to Fontaine-Dieudonné modules. Christol-Meboussat's theorem is extended to show that Evertse-Gabrielov-Azuma's theorem holds over $W[k]$, and within this context, a Berman-like differential equation is solved for both constant and non-constant coefficients.

This study explores the one-dimensional asymmetry in the angle between hadrons in SIDIS when using longitudinally polarized protons, specifically examining the difference in the distribution of hadron pairs. Calculations for this asymmetry are performed for events where two hadrons move in opposite directions and consider the influence of the helicity dependence of both the spin structure function and the hadron fragmentation. Our findings reveal that the hadron fragmentation contribution is minimal in events with opposite-moving hadrons but needs to be considered in future experiments. Additionally, our results indicate that the cos$\phi_R$ asymmetry is primarily driven by the difference in the longitudinal spin dependence of the hadron fragmentation function and can provide insights into the chiral odd twist-3 quark distribution. Utilizing only longitudinally polarized protons in SIDIS offers a more cost-effective means of studying quark spin distributions compared to using transversely polarized protons.

Eugene Fock made a significant contribution to general relativity by creating the so-called Fock metric, which could represent the material fields of the early universe in a de Sitter space.  His work further introduced the concept of conformal time, which is the basis for many modern de Sitter models.  A new approach has been taken to simplify the Einstein-field equations for a one-dimensional, spherically symmetric space, allowing for a more fundamental derivation of Fock's metric.  This approach has been shown to be equivalent to applying a specific mathematical transformation, which has been found to have de Sitter spacetime as one of its many variants.

This research focuses on linear symplectic transformations and their associated orthogonal symplectic transformations, known as OSSA for a given signature. We examine the conditions under which certain symplectic transformations can be converted into others, using specific classification schemes. Additionally, we have developed several mathematical criteria related to the parameters that define these classifications.

This paper proposes a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding representation for the hierarchical structure of Wikipedia. By converting Wikipedia into a layered graph, where each node is associated with a specific hierarchy level, and applying a graph neural network, we can learn entity embeddings. This approach leverages both the content of Wikipedia articles and its hierarchical organization to enhance entity representations. We demonstrate our method's efficacy through entity completion and pagination examples on the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, outperforming baseline methods in both tasks. Furthermore, we visually visualize the learned embeddings' capability to capture real-world entities by following Wikipedia's hierarchy.

The increasing number of patients waiting for kidney transplants has led to an urgent need for new organs. Researchers are focusing on crossmatching to improve the compatibility between donors and recipients, but this process can be costly and time-consuming. To reduce these expenses, we examine a decision-making process for a hospital that determines the optimal acceptance of previously unmatched kidneys that have become compatible due to prospective donors. This option, however, is limited by the hospital's capacity to perform the necessary tests. Our research provides a theoretical framework and practical policies for this scenario, taking into account new organs that are immediately compatible, as well as previously unmatched kidneys that become compatible. These insights can be applied to the crossmatching program and the utilization of donation after deceased donors (DDC).

This work presents an overview of the implicit ties research area, which explores the phenomenon where people's behavior is influenced by that of others without direct contact with peers. The research has been conducted across numerous contexts and employs a wide range of methodologies. Given the covert nature of these studies, this study aims to provide a comprehensive overview by summarizing the research designs used in implicit ties studies and outlining avenues for future exploration.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit linguistic patterns captured by these embeddings. We illustrate our theoretical concepts by analyzing the polarity of corporate financial reports from 1996 to 2016, obtained from the SEC's EDGAR database. The results indicate that NLP models are susceptible to the inherent structure and polarity inherent in these reports, often yielding outcomes that mirror the results of Loughran-McDonald's linear model. Our analysis suggests that NLP models do not provide a genuine resolution to the issues associated with financial report sentiment analysis, as their output is heavily influenced by the statistical patterns of the data, leading to predictable and less innovative findings.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents to the innovative
wideband waveforming technique proposed in Ref.1, which creates additional gain
in integrated data and energy transfer systems beyond what is achieved through
multi-antenna and multi-carrier configurations.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of both approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing the Cartesian grid, enabling an accurate and stable solution to the governing equations via a modified level-set method and a specialized embedded boundary treatment. This technique effectively handles complex boundary transformations, high curvature areas, and normal vector calculations. Level-set and embedded boundary methods are precisely reconstructed and solved, respectively, with appropriate numerical flux adjustments and enhanced solution recovery. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through various tests, including rapid changes in phase boundaries, boundary swirling, and interactions between multiple droplets.

Current theories of the mental lexicon suggest that words are interconnected, allowing for more efficient access. Words can be linked through various relationships, but studying unary connections, which involve a single word and operate like a spin, has been underrepresented. This type of connection is similar to the principles of quantum mechanics, where a word's state can be altered by thinking about associated features, such as color or shape changing a shape's shape. We propose an experiment to test the effect of unary connections on word retrieval, involving participants completing the Lexical Decision Task on words for 'spin' after being told about a related dimension, comparing this to a task with no spin, which would demonstrate the efficiency of unary connections and their parallel to quantum operations on word representation.

A study was conducted on the impact of preventive rewiring on graph theory, comparing it to random graph generation. The research focused on how the spread of an epidemic, modeled by the SIR framework, is affected by the introduction of new connections compared to the removal of old ones. It was discovered that the choice between increasing or decreasing the number of connections significantly influences the outcome, with the rapidest growth occurring when connections are removed, in contrast to the slower growth resulting from the addition of new connections. This research focuses on differential geometry, specifically on nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds and explores Cotton solitons in relation to Ricci-soliton flows.
We establish that under certain conditions, the flow of these manifolds will converge smoothly to a Torus or projective plane.
Additionally, we prove that if the manifold has a scalar curvature that is an eigenfunction of the Lee form, the flow will converge smoothly to a compact manifold and provide a similar result for anti-Tanaka-Webster flow.

This paper establishes a comprehensive framework that integrates the latest advances in quantum chromodynamics calculations, experimental measurements, and statistical assessments to support the development of up-to-date parton distribution functions through rigorous data fitting procedures.

To improve the efficiency of training, policy optimization methods like DDPG utilize a replay buffer that stores past experiences and retrieves them in random order during subsequent iterations. A common issue with the replay buffer is the risk of polluting the policy when experienced data is based on the current policy. This problem is exacerbated in continuous action spaces due to the high variance of the neural network. Although the replay buffer's capacity is typically large, most research has not given sufficient attention to the removal of relevant data from the buffer. This paper proposes an innovative variance diminution method, which involves strategically deleting selected experiences from the replay buffer in order to mitigate the variance of data and enhance policy optimization efficiency. Furthermore, we integrate the variance diminution method with the standard replay mechanism, resulting in the proposed variance-reweighted network (VRN). Our results on continuous policy optimization benchmarks indicate the effectiveness of VRN in boosting policy optimization efficiency.

Our analysis of the multi-band superconductor (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ combines angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and maximum entropy methods to examine its electronic structure and gap structure. Utilizing our measured data as a foundation, we employ a tight-binding model to mathematically describe the electron bands and, through this model, obtain the superconductor's gap structure. Our analysis indicates an electron-like sheet located approximately 1.0 eV below the $E$ axis that cannot be accounted for by the electron bands described by the tight-binding model. Furthermore, our maximum entropy method analysis reveals an unusual inner electron-like sheet that cannot be attributed to any superconducting gap splitting. Our findings suggest an unusual superconducting gap structure consisting of an inner hole-like sheet with a maximum gap size of approximately 4.5 meV, an unusual inner electron-like sheet with a maximum gap size of approximately 3.5 meV, and two outer electron-like sheets with maximum gap sizes of approximately 1.5 meV and 1.3 meV respectively.

Both the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization equation yield the same result: a macroscopic number of pairs in the D3 D7 quantum Hall model. We verify the equivalence of these two approaches through a detailed comparison, specifically using the free energy density at finite temperature for this model.

The study presents initial findings on the polarization of the top quark produced from a single $t$-channel process, which deviates from long-standing theoretical assumptions. By analyzing the angle between the top quark and the neutrino in the rest frame of the top quark, researchers can determine the degree of polarization. Specifically, the measurement of the distribution of the $\cos\theta^*$ variable indicates the extent of polarization. Comparing the data to theoretical models allows for a precise determination of the degree of polarization, which is found to be consistent with theoretical predictions.

The magnetic and metallic behavior of LaNiO$_3$ are modified within thin film and superlattice structures, yet adding reservoir layers of LaAlO$_3$ deepens and broadens its antiferromagnetic domain while expanding its Coer force, without affecting its critical temperature. Utilizing $\beta$-detected NMR, this study observes the distinct  $^8$Li spin precession in various LaAlO$_3$ /LaNiO$_3$ /LaAlO$_3$ sample libraries at different metallic and insulating states, and is correlated with electrical conductivity. It reveals that the LaO termination of the LaNiO$_3$ layers generates an in-plane electric field gradient leading to metallic behavior, in contrast to the LaAlO$_3$ /LaNiO$_3$ samples with the NiO$_2$ terminated LaNiO$_3$ layers that display an additional hyperfine interaction with a distinct metallic and an insulating population of $^8$Li.

In our analysis of conversational language, we face numerous possible responses 
to a single statement, which we believe has been poorly captured by current 
word-by-word prediction models. To address this limitation, we developed 
MultiTalk, a new dataset that challenges models to predict multiple dialogue 
continuations from a single sentence. Our method involves manually creating a 
rich conversation with an equally skilled human partner and then randomly 
selecting individual sentences to serve as context for the model. In contrast 
to existing datasets, our dataset not only features highly branched conversation 
trees but also provides extensive conversation details including all previous 
dialogue turns, topic information, and various sentence-level annotations. Our 
experiment shows that even with full model training and multiple augmentations, 
the model lags significantly behind a basic human model across multiple metrics. 
Furthermore, our analysis of the dataset reveals its potential for generating 
diverse and coherent conversations through techniques such as the beam search, 
which our existing models are incapable of achieving effectively.

This research analyzes and models the throughput of an erasable intelligent surface (EIS) assisted multi-input multi-output (MIMO) communication system to determine its performance capabilities. Specifically, this study evaluates the throughput in scenarios involving correlated signal fading and excludes ideal phase shift modeling often assumed in previous studies. Mathematical expressions for spectral and energy efficiency are derived, taking into account realistic conditions of energy supply, data transmission rates, and surface sizing. By utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, the study assesses the statistical behavior of spectral and energy efficiency, thereby providing valuable insights for optimizing such systems under realistic conditions.

We introduce MG-Fast, an efficient and simplified method to simulate N-body gravity beyond the standard model for large datasets. This method allows research groups to quickly test multiple modified gravity models in a consistent manner, saving considerable computational resources. By using MG-Fast, even the largest simulation datasets can be produced for various theories in a short period and with minimal computational costs, as demonstrated with the Euclid simulation. The program maintains key features of rigorous simulations while significantly reducing the computational time required, allowing for the creation of smooth, real-world applicable datasets. The MG-Fast framework allows for the simulation of different modified gravity models by adding specific theory components to the standard gravitational matrix, as opposed to changing the underlying theory. This modularity enables the creation of high-quality datasets for various scenarios, as demonstrated with simulations of $\Lambda$CDM, $f(R)$ gravity, and scalar-tensor-spice models. The MG-Fast code is implemented in C++ and can be run on minimal computational resources, as long as it can interface with Gadget-4. The detailed documentation of the program is available on the GitHub repository.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface, connecting with multiple stochastic Loewner evolution, by equating it with the Gaussian free field. This framework enables the representation of conformal loop ensembles. This concept was limited to cases where the number of SLEs was finite. In this research, a framework was introduced that expands this framework to include an 'gas' of Chordal SLE$_\kappa$, by utilizing the stochastic Loewner evolution, while taking into consideration the repulsive interactions between the drivers, while maintaining the connection with the Gaussian free field, which could represent conformal loop ensembles, $\mathcal{CLE}_\kappa(d)$. This research involved solving a pathwise optimization problem to determine the equilibrium measure, while involving large deviations principles, while involving dynamic variants of the Riemann zeta function, Christoffel-Szego polynomials, and Hecke operators.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source derivation designed as a collaborative
research platform. Derived from MediaWiki, WorkingWiki incorporates the same core
functionality while offering the added benefit of a read-only, static HTML output.
This feature is particularly useful for presenting finalized results to a wider
audience, as seen in the case study of the WorkingPeriodsWiki project. Despite initial
differences in database structure and software dependencies, extending the core MediaWiki
functionality to WorkingWiki is a straightforward process. Furthermore, the
periodicity analysis case study has been accomplished with minimal use of Python, with
only numpy and scipy required, with other libraries optional due to the retention of the
original PHP processing framework.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a turbulent jet flame to determine its heat release rate fluctuations and their response to acoustic perturbations. To simplify the problem, an active flame model is utilized. Upon solving the governing equations for quiescent conditions using one-dimensional steady-state profiles, small acoustic disturbances are introduced into the ambient environment. To efficiently solve for the fluctuating heat release rate, an existing code is modified through the implementation of an active flame module. Furthermore, the resulting solution is verified through a case study that replicates conditions from a laboratory experiment. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, one additional case is simulated in which the reaction rates are altered to simulate an flame that is approaching quenching, in contrast to an stable flame.

We present a novel technique for detecting multiple aspects of dynamic and unified chimera states in networks of interacting oscillators. This method is applicable to any type of dynamical system and does not require knowledge of the underlying equation, while effectively identifying and differentiating between various states of unity, partial synchronization, and the type of synchronization that exists. By utilizing this technique, we were able to examine the impact of mean field coupling on a network of Type 2 integrate-and-fire neurons, discovering three distinct states of synchronization (unit, quasi, and clustered) along with their characteristics. Furthermore, this method provided a clear way to measure the different types of synchronization within the network.

Our new variant of the 2D Ising model is based on a 2D lattice graph, where the probability of an adjacent pair of sites both containing 'up' or 'down' spins is higher than that of opposite-oriented spins. This parameter varies between 0 and 1. As the temperature decreases, the system exhibits a continuous phase transition at a critical temperature greater than zero, evidencing critical exponents and universality. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal clusters forming within the system, with their size escalating as the system approaches the critical point, showcasing cluster percolation. Notably, this occurs beyond the critical temperature and involves clusters connected through 'up-up' or 'down-down' bonds.

We investigate the impact of ultralight dark matter on neutrinoless double beta decay oscillations and related experiments. Neutrino oscillations are influenced by their coherent motion through the dark matter graces, and if the wavelength of this oscillation is comparable to the size of the Earth, their decay experiment is affected. In such instances, the experiment observes the superposition of signals from varying locations and times, and even the orientation of detectors could affect results. However, this effect isn't confusing; it simply provides additional data to inform our understanding of neutrino masses and mixing angles. Given that the ULDM may include significant components in the eV scale, we explore another potential effect: the decoupling of the ULDM from the Higgs field and the resulting precession of neutrino flavors as they propagate. This has implications for both neutrino experiments and the early universe's evolution, and we constrain the interaction between neutrinos and ULDM based on data from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and neutrino experiments.

Existing models for predicting the flux of ultra-high energy photons arriving at the Earth from the Sun have not been comprehensively studied. We examine the effects of the Sun's magnetic field and solar wind on these photons during their journey to the Earth, considering different levels of plasma frequency. Our findings suggest that models based on the hadronic flux could inaccurately predict the flux of ultra-high energy photons by up to two orders of magnitude due to the Sun's magnetic field. We develop and present simplified yet effective models to more accurately forecast the ultra-high energy photon flux observed from the Sun.

Nonlocal gravity research is advancing, but it faces a challenge in comparing different theories due to the presence of nonlocal terms in both the action and the field equations. To address this, we introduce a general framework to convert nonlocal operators into local ones using a fundamental frame, thereby creating an equivalent local theory for each theory of gravity. This approach reveals interesting implications, such as multiple "matter-like" fields emerging from nonlocality, some with inverted-sign kinetic energy, and others with multiple components possessing both positive and negative energy. It also represents an opportunity to test nonlocal gravity theories by observing specific combinations of gravitational waves and cosmological constants.

Conflicting writes to the same memory address in a replicated data structure lead to segmentation issues that can compromise system reliability. Converting orderless event delivery into sequential access patterns is crucial for maintaining consistency, but it's often insufficient due to the operation's associativity. Many conversion methods exclude concurrent operations, hindering performance and causing system inefficiencies. To address this challenge, we propose the Remove-Win design framework, a conflict-free replicated data structure (CRDS) approach for non-blocking, wait-free systems. This framework permits simultaneous operations as long as there are no conflicting writes to the same memory location, resulting in optimized conversion complexities and enhanced performance. The framework includes a set of techniques to manage conflicts, including:
   - Conflict avoidance through index management,
   - Conflict exclusion through index expansion and tree reorganization,
   - Conflict resolution via index adjustment and value replacement,
   - Conflict elimination through index modification and value merging.
We validated the framework's design principles by developing five conflict-free data structure algorithms, including sort maps, skip lists, hash tables, arrays, and prefix trees. These implementations exhibit optimal or near-optimal time complexities for various operations, including search, insertion, and deletion. The framework's performance and efficiency are further highlighted by experimental comparisons with state-of-the-art CRDSs and real-world system deployments, demonstrating reduced overhead and improved performance. The framework's design principles and technical details are outlined in the accompanying supplementary material.

Functional genomics offers in-depth insights into the molecular mechanisms that drive the organization and functionality of the human genome. Evaluating large-scale functional genomics datasets in relation to human trait-associated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) through genome-wide association studies (GWAS) can enhance our understanding of the genetic underpinnings of complex human characteristics. In this research, we explore 18 diverse human traits encompassing blood, growth, metabolism, and reproduction, by comparing functional annotation across the human genome with SNPs from extensively powered GWAS. We discovered an enrichment of genetic variants associated with human traits in regions of the genome marked by high conservation, open chromatin, and cell-type-specific enhancer marks. Notably, there is substantial overlap between genetic variants that influence the proteome and those that affect various human characteristics. A key implication of this study is the benefit of integrating functional genomics and GWAS when exploring human complexity.

This thesis has studied rare events in quantum field theory known as "minor incidents," specifically focusing on the unique environment of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). These events are significant because they offer a closer look at the intricate dynamics of high-energy particle collisions. 

While the analysis presented here is focused on eye-catching examples, it serves as well-suited material for an instructional presentation or educational seminar. The material can be utilized to introduce the LHC's experimental settings and the theoretical underpinnings of quantum field theory to those new to the subject. Furthermore, it can be adapted to explore more subdued incidents upon examining lepton flavor violation in the LC$_{\rm mu}$, providing insight into the nuances of studying these complex dynamics.

A well-known characteristic of low-mass X-ray binaries is their quiescent periods, which vary in length and follow an irregular pattern. Researchers generally agree that the distribution of these periods in this class of binaries is self-similar. In contrast, there is a lack of data on neutron star LMXBs near the Milky Way's center in recent decades. Some hypotheses suggest they have shorter accretion periods than PSR 1135-19, the shortest known Neutron star LMXB in this region. Analysis of optical emissions from the white dwarf in these systems also indicates they could have even shorter recurrence periods. However, our observations of these systems during possible short-term intervals in past records and using Chandra X-ray observations of the area's infrared sources with the Ariel 3 and Fermi-LAT catalogs of pulsars conclude that two of the quiescent X-ray sources could in fact be the shortest-period NS LMXBs in the Milky Way's center. Furthermore, optical measurements of the companion stars in these systems don't contradict this finding.

The dynamics of a particular category of celestial bodies known as wide binaries is unusually disruptive, prompting some researchers to misinterpret the significance of a specific anomaly in their data. This study seeks to clarify the implications of wide binary data by presenting an overly simplified model that still captures the key feature in question. We overcome previous limitations associated with binary systems by utilizing an ensemble model, in contrast to the typical practice of analyzing single systems. This in turn allows us to more accurately evaluate evidence for modifying general relativity based on observations of wide binaries. We define specific performance metrics essential for gravitational theory, rather than relying solely on orbital data fitting. As anticipated, general relativity fails to meet these criteria, surpassing a specific threshold by a significant margin, in agreement with the conclusions of a previous study using a more complex model. However, our wording is more restrained than its predecessor, in line with the principle of not assuming more than the data supports. On the other hand, we find that several alternatives to general relativity fall even shorter of the necessary criteria, in contrast to wide binary data, in a manner similar to eddingtonization. This implies that, if supported by wider binary data, specific modified theories of gravity may exhibit an excess of coherence by multiple margins, surpassing that of a specific dark matter halo by about three to four times.

Radio sources powered by the activity of nearby galaxies' accretion and nuclear processes are classified as active galactic nuclei-powered radio sources. Understanding their properties is crucial due to their relatively low brightness, which constitutes approximately 10% of the background infrared source population at 8 microns. Combining radio and infrared data from ATLAS3 and Steward's Megamap in the near-infrared allows us to investigate the relationship between radio and infrared properties as a function of angular size. Using stacking analysis, we discovered an 18 micron brightness temperature gradient, which decreases by 1 decade per 2 decades in angular scale. This indicates that radio sources are generally brighter and more abundant in smaller scales, which when converted to a 1 MHz bandwidth, correlates with previous radio spectral index measurements of compact radio sources. Additionally, analyzing the radio sources' spectral energy distributions (SEDs) as a function of angular scale, we determined that larger-scale sources are hotter than compact ones, which when converted to a 1 MHz bandwidth, matches the radio spectral index measurements. This indicates that the thermochromic effect plays a significant role in determining SEDs of AGN-powered radio sources. Moreover, comparing the infrared spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of radio sources and the general infrared source population, we found that radio sources are dustier than the typical infrared sources across all scales. On scales less than angular scales of 0.2 arcseconds, the difference in infrared spectral properties becomes indistinguish

We analyze the impact of sound waves on shock waves rising through expanding, ejected mass during supernovae and massive star eruptions, where the jet is initially subsonic. It's common for intense quasi-monochromatic acoustic waves to result from quasi-periodic oscillations in the supernovae progenitors or central engines. The interaction of these waves with the shock wave leads to significant fluctuations in the shock velocity. However, the envelope's expansion rate largely remains unaffected by this interaction, as the ejected mass accelerates to a similar speed within one period, regardless of whether the shock is being reinforced by the waves or has passed it. This nearly sonar-like interaction between waves and shock wave has a minimal impact on the early dynamics of the shock wave and its transmission efficiency. Nevertheless, the intense quasi-monochromatic waves contribute to a nearly periodic variation in the shock's brightness, as the energy transmitted per unit of time remains largely independent of whether the shock is being reinforced by the waves or has passed it.

We provide a new framework to exclude non-mathematical algebraic functions that can mislead in algebraic modularity theorems, and offer a geometric analog of this theory. Specifically, we define algebraic functions that satisfy algebraic modularity theorems as "mathematical" within our framework, and establish sufficient conditions for this categorization, including for non-algebraic analytic functions. Furthermore, we explore the functions' algebraic or non-mathematical nature from a geometric perspective.

Connections between electrons and their environment, such as phonons, lead to important effects like energy transfer and loss, which are highly relevant for novel devices using superconductivity, magnetism, and quantum states in solids. To truly understand these interactions, particularly those involving phonons at a material's surface, it is necessary to study how they vary with momentum. By analyzing thin films of lead and aluminum, the research presents high-resolution data that reveals the combined influence of phonons on electrons across different momenta. This provides a clear map of how electrons scatter due to phonon interaction, which changes substantially when considering the electron's momentum and shows substantial differences between materials.

$\tau$-tilting theory, which originated from the theory of tilting, has been integrated into representation theory and wild quiver representation. This introduction aims to provide a thorough explanation of $\tau$-tilting theory, including its fundamental properties and various applications, and we have aimed to supply the necessary technical details to make this introduction accessible to those with a background in basic homological algebra. Furthermore, we have examined and presented the connections between $\tau$-tilting theory and two distinct areas: cluster tilting, and tilting by mutation.

The success of task-oriented dialogue systems relies on them producing natural, purpose-driven responses that align with conversation goals. This paper investigates whether current NLI models capture the diversity of human meanings in non-compelled conversations. Three experiments were conducted assessing whether single-semantics predictions by NLI satisfy a semantic diversity measure for human dialogues, first with static semantic representations and subsequently with large language model-based representations. A benchmark called Neural Semantic Diversity in Dialogue (N-SDD) was introduced to evaluate this criterion. While using NLI to model dialogue semantically does enhance diversity compared to ignoring intent, it falls short of natural human semantics in terms of variety. This finding suggests further improvement is needed in how machine-semantics is interpreted.

Automated driving systems require evaluating risks during lane changes, which involves identifying potential dangers in nearby traffic. This task can be complex due to the need to process short video clips and quickly identify hazardous actions of other drivers. To tackle this challenge, a new approach is proposed that uses a two-stage deep neural network to predict behavior and classify it as safe or hazardous. The proposed network uses the Star-Net architecture, which is known for its efficiency in processing video data and its ability to transfer segmentation masks. Tests using the BViD dataset show that this approach outperforms existing methods and achieves a reliable accuracy of 84% in identifying hazardous actions.

The potential for precise astrometry in astronomical imaging has been achieved through sophisticated algorithms, allowing submillisecond precision in star position measurement. This breakthrough allows for precise determination of orbital parameters in planetary systems, particularly near their stability limits. This study presents a method to simulate three-dimensional rotating objects in binary systems, taking into consideration mass-shedding effects. This method is applied to estimate the precision with which substellar objects' spin periods and binary parameters can be measured using astrometry, allowing for precise measurements up to high-mass binary systems with near 2.2 solar masses. These precise measurements occur at limits where the object's spin period closely matches its binary partner's, potentially exposing surface features like hot spots. This allows for accurate determination of the object's rotation as it orbits, however, issues with accuracy can still persist even with precise data. This study demonstrates the potential of astrometry for characterizing substellar objects in binary systems, offering accurate precision models for one-mass-shedding objects up to high-mass binary systems.

In particle physics experiments, hadron production is often studied through amplitude analyses which involve modeling interactions between particles to explain angular and mass distribution patterns. However, several instrumental and non-instrumental factors can influence this data, necessitating their correct handling within the amplitude models used. This note introduces a general approach to a specific problem, allowing for a more effective use of experimental information while avoiding overinterpretation, and it also outlines the key requirements for successful implementation. Two examples from CERFIT and LELEBACCO analyses are provided to illustrate the proposed method.

A significant number of High-z Gamma-ray bursts and their afterglows have been observed through the LIGO gravitational wave detections, necessitating a refined theory to explain this phenomenon. Existing afterglow models have shown various discrepancies in their data points when plotted on logarithmic scales. This research presents a new, universally applicable model that accounts for both the early and late-stage viscous fireball phases, occurring before and after the adiabatic transition point. The results indicate that highly conductive plasma follows this universal model, whereas the less conductive plasma adheres to a different, multi-stage model in its intermediate stage.

We've developed a new approach to efficiently resolve the bipartite vertex splitting problem within a parameter $k$. Our method demonstrates that identifying if a given graph $G$ can be transformed into a bipartite graph by separating vertices that are part of a $k$-sized parameter is tractable. This resolution is achieved through a running time of approximately $10^{4.5} \cdot k^2$ milliseconds, coupled with uses of memory amounting to $2^{6.5} \cdot k^{3.5}$ kilobytes.

Deep neural network-based recognition systems have been successfully applied in real-world scenarios, yet their performance starts to decline when they encounter new categories in their class distribution. While learning vectors from new categories is feasible using continuous incremental learning algorithms, these methods are ineffective without labeled data for all possible categories. To address situations where data for novel categories is unavailable, researchers have developed incremental algorithms that selectively focus on important categories by prioritizing balance in class representation. Despite reported promising results of such algorithms, their robustness in learning vector spaces for imbalanced scenarios remains unconfirmed due to lack of thorough evaluation. This study explores the complexity of incorporating new categories in balance-inclined incremental algorithms and investigates the impact of calibration techniques on their performance through comparative analysis of multiple approaches, employing both logistic regression and quadratic programming methods. Our findings suggest that incorporating a stringent calibration method is essential to ensure the reliability and validity of the learned vector space.

This paper presents the thruster-assisted bipedal locomotion framework, a set of gait generation methods tailored for bipedal robots capable of efficient and stable walking. Initially, we demonstrate that efficient binary gaits can be achieved by utilizing minimal thruster force, which can be generated using a proposed model. Subsequently, we propose an optimization approach to refine these forces, taking into account real-world constraints such as maximum available thrust and robot balance. The proposed framework includes two key features: (1) efficient binary gait generation, and (2) precise balance maintenance during flight phases, enabling unique advantages over traditional legged locomotion methods. The framework's performance is validated through the development of two prototype robots with limited thrust capacity, showcasing their capacity to perform efficient walks on flat surfaces and navigate challenging inclines.

Let $A$ be an integral domain that's valued in a additive total residue class group. We investigate how this property passes down to integral extensions of $A$, assuming they're finitely generated, and discuss its implications for certain types of domains like those with finite or additive total unit groups.

Modern multi-core processors, despite their efficiency, are constrained by thermal limits that prevent further increases in computational performance. Although increasing the number of cores continuously enhances performance, it comes with rising costs and diminishing returns on performance per dollar spent. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel, non-invasive technique called Hyperdegradation, which involves lowering the CPU's operating frequency to achieve optimal performance. By doing so, we were able to surpass the performance of high-core-count systems and even single CPUs running at their maximum frequency, without incurring any additional costs or requiring hardware modifications. Our method involves building highly adaptable testbeds capable of varying both the number of allocated cores and the CPU's operating frequency, allowing us to analyze and characterize systems with granularity. Through Hyperdegradation, we were able to increase performance by nearly a factor of three relative to single CPUs running at their maximum frequency, involving systems with as few as four cores operating at reduced frequencies. Systems hyperdegraded in this manner also exhibit excellent performance per dollar and performance per watt efficiency scores. To facilitate wider adoption of Hyperdegradation, we released the HyperDegrade Library, enabling researchers to precisely control the number of allocated cores and CPU frequencies, thereby facilitating the fine-grained experimentation necessary for innovating new techniques like Hyperdegradation.

We examine the potential of using the electroweak sector of the Standard Model as a tool to resolve the discrepancy between the experimental and standard model predictions for the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. In the initial analysis, the contribution to this parameter from within the Standard Model, specifically tied to the Higgs boson, is found to be inconsistent with the magnitude of the discrepancy. A more in-depth investigation involving modifications to the Higgs sector reveals specific conditions under which the discrepancy might be resolved. In particular, we discover that adding four heavy quark sectors with mass surpassing the Higgs boson leads to a resolution within a narrow range of the Higgs coupling to these quarks, whereas resolving the puzzle by adding two vector-like quarks requires them to have specific, unusually light masses which contradicts current experimental data from LHC.

This study determines the angle gamma of the penguin from decays of particles produced in collisions, specifically from branch-level decisions. Data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and with an integrated luminosity of 139 $^{-1}$ pb from experiments D0 and Diode are used to analyze direct CP asymmetries in various decay modes: $B^0 \to \pi^0\pi^0$, $B^0 \to \pi^+\pi^-$, $B^+ \to \pi^+\pi^-$, and $B^0 \to K^0\bar{K}^0$. Direct CP asymmetries are calculated from time-dependent or time-undependent analyses, incorporating measurements from both experiments for each decay mode. From these data, we derive constraints on the parameters of the penguin, including the ratio of direct CP asymmetries $R_{\pi\pi}$ and mixing-induced CP asymmetry $S_{\pi\pi}$ in certain decays, as well as the magnitude and phase of the penguin amplitude $R_K$, $ \phi_R$ in $B^0 \to K^0\bar{K}^0$ decays.

We propose a discrete entangling operation that generalizes previous methods to include welded chord diagrams. This proposal accounts for disentangling and separating connected diagrams, and we demonstrate its application through the analysis of the 2-solitaire link.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve $\Gamma$ over a semifield $K$ is finitely generated over the tropical semifield $\mathbb{T}^+$. Specifically, there exists a finite set of pairs $(s_\lambda, f_\lambda)$ in $E(\Gamma \times \mathbb{T}) \times F(\Gamma)$ such that the rational function semifield $F(\Gamma)$ is generated by the set $\{f_\lambda | \lambda \in \Lambda\}$ and the set $\{s_\lambda |_ \Gamma | \Lambda\}$, where $\Lambda$ is a finite index set. This result implies that the field of rational functions of a tropical curve has a finite basis.

We've demonstrated that I^3 can be defined using classical knot theory tools,
specifically an invariant of the Fox-Hatcher loop, which aligns with previous
findings by singularity theory when applied to the standard knot knot. We've also
discovered that defining the triple point singularity contribution requires the
Fox-Hatcher loop contribution.

The recent research by KATRIN has established a rigorous upper bound on electron anti-neutrino mass with high confidence, yet it doesn't provide a comparable limit in the other mass spectrum. This study aims to investigate the potential lower bounds on neutrino masses based on oscillation data, which necessitates an understanding of the absolute neutrino mass spectrum. Specifically, it uses the most recent KATRIN results and oscillation data to analyze the feasible range of one-neutrino and three-neutrino scenarios, as well as various three-neutrino extension theories.

Matrix multiplication in linear algebra is a fundamental operation that many computational fields rely on. Given its intensive computational nature, utilizing the Central Processing Unit (CPU) or Graphical Processing Unit (GPU) can significantly accelerate the process. This paper examines both CPU and GPU approaches to matrix multiplication, comparing their efficiencies through practical experiments. By analyzing various matrix sizes, our study demonstrates the advantages of GPU-based multiplication in terms of time reduction, thus educating students on the fundamentals of GPU programming in a hands-on manner.

In many real-world applications, multiple robotic agents need to coordinate their actions to move in unison according to a pre-set plan. To achieve this efficiently, the robots must not only synchronize with one another but also optimize the energy consumed by moving and communicating. A key challenge arises when designing a system that allows the robots to reach a state of synchronized action while taking into consideration their individual movements and communication costs, all while avoiding unnecessary complexity. The proposed solution involves a innovative approach using a specifically structured network of robots, where the connectivity follows a ring-like pattern. This approach has been proven to be sufficient for synchronization purposes, reducing connectivity costs by up to a factor of N compared to other methods. Furthermore, a cooperative algorithm is developed to enable the robots to reach a state of synchronized action while consuming less energy and avoiding the need to explicitly estimate the number of agents involved. The proposed system offers the advantage of being both optimal in terms of energy consumption and capable of reducing synchronization errors by a significant margin.

To address the limitations of rate calculations for future experiments and astronomical observations, high-precision computations in quantum field theory are increasingly important. The necessity of such computations is particularly evident in cosmological studies and celestial observations, where extracting precise information about the theory's fundamental components, such as its components and growth, is challenging due to the presence of infrared divergences in perturbation theory. Perturbative expansions in quantum field theories converge slowly as the infrared sector is not properly controlled, often hindering predictions. The proposed method of amplitude-based resummation addresses this issue, allowing the isolation and precise handling of the infrared sector to enable accurate predictions for observable quantities, such as cross-sections and scattering amplitudes, and potentially even influencing the initial conditions of cosmic evolution. This paper provides a detailed explanation of the amplitude-based resummation program, as well as its current capabilities and potential, and discusses possible extensions, such as incorporating quantum gravitational effects, which could be relevant for future space missions and observational capabilities, as well theoretical implications.

Vertical federated learning (VFL) enables high-risk industry sectors like finance and healthcare to collaborate and develop joint machine learning models without sharing their raw data. By contributing to the training of a joint model, participants can gain access to more data and more accurate information than they would have had they trained a model on their own. However, VFL is vulnerable to privacy breaches, allowing attackers to reclaim up to 82% of their data under certain circumstances and 55% of the data from other participating parties. We have discovered these defenses can be undermined with two novel attacks tailored for VFL. First, we developed an algorithm to directly attack a neural network by using a proxy model and by manipulating the input data. Then, we created an algorithm that targets a gradient-based training process and that is capable of accurately identifying up to 82% of the data of an attacker and 55% of the data of other participating parties. These findings highlight the necessity for robust privacy protection techniques, especially in sectors like finance and healthcare where participants are contributing sensitive information to the training of a machine learning model.

Kernel methods are widely used in various Bayesians modeling techniques, particularly for smoothing and estimating densities. Although there are existing approaches like Random Fourier Features that approximate such methods, they suffer from inaccuracies in density estimation as they add more features, due to their assumption of i.i.d. data, which often doesn't hold for data requiring smoothing. We propose an alternative approach in this paper, where the estimation of functions and densities is customized to specific data by creating an efficient, low-dimensional representation and transforming it into a set of complex numbers. We show our approach to be computationally comparable to RFF yet superior in accuracy, outperforming both it and traditional kernel methods in terms of efficiency and accuracy in Fourier transformation.

In our study, we found the maximum group that can be faithfully embedded in a group $G^{n}\wr S_{m}$, where $G$ is a group and $S_{m}$ is the symmetric group of degree $m$, by analyzing groups by their Cartesian structure.

This research extends the application of Möbius transformations to conformally flat hypersurfaces of higher dimensions, focusing on those with constant curvature. We have established the existence of a Möbius invariant that can be expressed using the trace of the shape operator's third derivative. Specifically, for conformally flat hypersurfaces within the sphere, we show that any Mobius equivalent instance of a constant scalar curvature can be achieved through a sequence of transformations and a specific transformation. Additionally, we establish that any two such equivalent instances of a conformally flat and constant scalar curvature can be deformed into each other while maintaining their properties.

Accurately identifying heart structures from medical images is a crucial surgical planning tool, and automatic segmentation methods have been widely used for this purpose. These methods have been extensively studied and successfully applied to analyze normal cardiac function. Nevertheless, their performance in patients with rare, complex congenital heart diseases remains untested. This study evaluates the extent to which algorithms developed for normal cardiac function can be utilized to analyze blood flow patterns in patients with operator-dependent data from cardiac magnetic resonance studies. By utilizing operators' annotations on cardiac function and by simulating flow patterns, the researchers developed and evaluated a dataset consisting of 40 training and 10 testing images based on operator-annotated data. By utilizing advanced convolutional neural network technology, U-Net was trained to analyze cardiac function and blood flow patterns. The results showed excellent results for cardiac function, with high sensitivity and specificity scores, but the method struggled to accurately detect smaller areas in patients with complex heart diseases. Manual treatment of these areas was necessary to achieve the best performance. By comparing different dataset configurations, researchers found that a combination of cardiac function and blood flow patterns yielded the most promising results. The researchers also evaluated whether it was feasible to utilize lower image resolution to reduce scanning time, but the results indicated that this approach led to lower accuracy scores. The study highlights the need to develop novel evaluation metrics tailored to clinical needs and to establish standardized protocols for assessing the accuracy of medical imaging algorithms when analyzing complex cardiac diseases.

In recent years, the volume of data available for processing by high-performance computers is increasing at a rapid pace, especially in the field of materials science. The abundance of existing datasets can be leveraged to develop sophisticated models capable of capturing the complex relationship between microstructure and material properties in a wide range of applications, from phase-field modeling to fluid dynamics and heat transfer. The primary challenge encountered is the significant computational cost associated with training such models on complex, high-dimensional problems. To overcome this hurdle, researchers are turning to novel training algorithms and techniques for domain adaptation, aimed at reducing the amount of high-fidelity training required. The ultimate objective is to create models that are efficient and accurate enough to be utilized as surrogates in multi-physics simulations involving microstructurally complex materials. The development of such models would enable the prediction of material properties from microstructural analysis obtained from experimental techniques such as electron backscatter diffraction and computer tomography. The present work aims to build upon existing research in this area and present the necessary steps for a successful outcome. The author also introduces a innovative approach to reducing the amount of high-fidelity training required, utilizing machine learning from imperfect data generated from simple numerical simulations. The author demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique on the degradation of a linear elastic material into a viscous material.

A novel SWIPT-capable wireless system is considered in a novel wireless environment. In this environment, a wireless access point is able to supply data to multiple non-cognitive devices and also charge those devices using superimposed power beams within the WLAN. We develop a model to manage SWIPT networks and create an objective function with constraints to optimally allocate channel and power resources. The aim is to either maximize network data transfer or charging efficiency. The formulated problem is resolved via a branch-and-cut technique, extending an existing effective method by adding and branching on optimal solutions to modified sub-problems. The resulting algorithm exhibits near-optimal results in a short time, demonstrating the potential for real-world use after carefully tuning the time parameter. Numerical results show the model's ability to allocate more resources for either data transfer or charging in certain network scenarios.

Complex systems, comprising numerous individuals interacting under specific rules, are best studied through conditionally periodic systems. Research into these systems has often focused on specific extremes. However, a broader investigation exploring the full spectrum of extremal characteristics within various systemic conditions is lacking. Our research aims to establish a comprehensive framework to examine a complex condition by analyzing its most and least favorable aspects. We achieve this through investigating the maximum and minimum expressions of a particular condition's function. Specifically, we investigate the full spectrum of extremal expressions of a negative binomial binomial convolution distribution by analyzing its highest and lowest conditions. Notably, our study reveals that the minimum expression cannot be represented by a standard mathematical function but can be approximated using series expansions under certain conditions.

We aim to improve the performance of IEDIS, a current BWD model, by developing a more advanced model named BGloss. Building upon the H Huang et al. model, BGloss incorporates a sense-specific head and leverages pre-trained BERT embeddings. Unlike H Huang et al., we employ a different loss function and initialize the sense-specific head with random values. BGloss extends the BERT framework by integrating additional guidance from word definitions via a pre-trained dictionary model, allowing for more comprehensive word sense differentiation.

A significant number of everyday tasks and operations across various fields depend heavily on visual instructional materials.  These materials, which are often called multimodal procedures or guides, are widely used in fields such as industry, science, education, and consumer knowledge.  To make these guides more effective, producing high-quality sequencing of multistep processes is essential, especially when considering that people naturally group tasks into sequences based on factors like cause and effect, time, and spatial arrangements.  Current research on procedural knowledge sequencing primarily focuses on areas like industrial processes, scientific procedures, and cooking procedures, leaving the broader applicability and core aspects of people's knowledge in this domain somewhat unclear.  This paper initially explores people's underlying knowledge of sequential procedures in multiple domains through carefully designed experiments and then identifies the central features of people's knowledge by analyzing multimodal guides created for those domains.  This research offers a foundational step toward developing comprehensive theories of people's sequential knowledge across a wide range of situations and processes.

The study examines the characteristics of the "2-finger" branching process, a simplified model of the avalanche size in the crackling noise phenomenon. A key finding from this analysis is the derivation of the probability distribution for avalanche magnitudes, which differs from previous results obtained for a two-dimensional Ising model on a square lattice. To validate its theoretical results, the study employs a numerical simulation based on a randomized algorithm for this system.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials satisfying the airy differential equation are examined, and connections with moments and three-term recurrence relations are established. Certain unit lower triangular matrices that generalize the moment and alpha matrices are studied in the context of airy polynomials. Additional properties of these matrices and their relation to modified airy polynomials are demonstrated.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors is limited by quantum noise in power recycling cavities, whose length must be much greater than that of the main interferometer. The proposed implementation of a sloshing Sagnac interferometer for the power recycling region could significantly improve this sensitivity with its unique property of being short wavelength compatible, achieved by orienting the circulating light wavelength perpendicular to the recycling cavity length. Theoretical modeling and simulation using standard parameters for next-generation detectors demonstrate that introducing a pair of sloshing Sagnac interferometers could increase strain sensitivity by at least one order of magnitude at frequencies above 100 Hz.

In high-density deployments, an xFace (xMIMO) system utilizes laterally arranged antenna panels to improve uplink communication by dividing users into disjointed visibility panels. However, this paper tackles an overlooked challenge: users belonging to neighboring panels may still interfere with each other due to their randomly located system boundaries, which vary across applications. The author addresses this unresearched problem by formulating it as a non-intersecting random walk, aiming to enable users within the same panel to share radio resources without interference through a new protocol called uplink random access. The author also derives a closed closed-form expression for a specific case and a efficient approximation for general cases, accounting for panel size and starting positions. The expression/approximation proves beneficial in designing optimal air-interface protocols to minimize signaling overhead in resource allocation. Numerical simulations demonstrate the accuracy of the derived expression and approximation, while the analytical models provide valuable design guidelines by revealing key driving factors of panel disjointness without extensive simulations.

Recent observations and simulations have highlighted the significance of vertical shear instability (VSI) in protoplanetary disks, suggesting that VSI might be responsible for restricting disk extension and suppressing particle migration, thereby explaining the scarcity of massive gas planets. The development of VSI is thought to destroy the smooth structure of disks and create complex substructures such as surface patterns and dense midplanes. These characteristics of disks受VSI的影响, however, have not yet been fully explored. A high-resolution simulation, where the gravitational effects and VSI were properly considered, allowed us to investigate the structural features of a disk surface and midplane at a characteristic time, and to conduct theoretical observations, particularly in the dust continuum. The results revealed that VSI leads to the formation of surface patterns, while its non-linear development leads to excessive turbulence and surface mixing. Additionally, VSI results in the concentration of dust within the midplanes, and this has significant implications for the formation of massive rocky planets.

We treat on-site correlations and p-d couplings within DMFT in a Hamiltonian framework, allowing us to adjust parameters and examine their impact on the system. This research focuses on creating a Molmer-Sorensen gate using trapped ions that is not influenced by shifts in frequency. We modify the standard method to include frequency balancing between two adjacent trapped ions. By using three different laser frequencies and applying the standard method in expanded form, we can contribute equally to the gate operation from two separate trapped-modes for each ion. A crucial factor in this approach is ensuring that the frequency differences are related in a specific rational ratio. As a result of this method, the gate duration can be significantly decreased, independent of changes in frequency, which is an essential requirement for the development of scalable ion-qubit connected gates and cluster states production in trapped-ion systems.

Recent research has revealed that perovskite materials near their ferroelectric transition exhibit unusual motion of atoms within the crystal lattice. To understand this behavior, we analyzed the movement of atoms in titanium dioxide, barium zinc perovskite, and strontium titanate using high-speed, in-situ X-ray scattering techniques. An advanced model of these materials' structure was created, which showed that clusters of atoms in motion have a specific symmetry and vary in size. This dynamic behavior is directly linked to the formation of a disordered state in perovskite materials. Our findings provide a clearer understanding of structural dynamics at the atomic level and may guide the creation of highly functional new materials.

Conducting the experiment on cerium rhodate and collecting data on its structure, properties, and magnetic characteristics reveals intriguing similarities between this compound and a theoretically predicted strongly correlated Dirac metal.  To verify the status of cerium rhodate as a strongly correlated Dirac metal, we develop a GWA-level forecast for this material, incorporating its electronic structure modeled by the SLM, and we demonstrate that observations of its optical conductivity can be explained by the theory if we consider the strong correlations within the material.

We have developed an innovative statistical framework for analyzing data that exhibit bimodality, addressing a gap in existing theories and models. This framework utilizes a unique approach, combining a Bimodal rate and a Bimodal proportion, to characterize and analyze such data. Bimodal proportions distinguish between two groups within the population, while bimodal rates capture the relative frequencies occurring around specific values. This framework can be seen as a dual-aspect perspective, incorporating elements from unimodal and mixed distributions. Given this framework, we have derived direct implications, including an overall mean, variance-covariance matrix, and potential skewness, thereby enabling a comprehensive examination of bimodal systems. Moreover, we have created a novel Bimodal Rate and Proportion (BRP) test to detect bimodality in various contexts, demonstrating its robustness and performance through an extensive simulation study. Furthermore, the framework has significant real-world applications, which we have illustrated through two detailed case studies, analyzing an extensive dataset from a long-term ecological research site and a smaller dataset from a medical study on Alzheimer's disease.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to detect a specific type of hypothetical particle called a heavy neutral lepton. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays, they determined the best possible limits on how long this particle would survive, depending on its mass within a specific range. By replicating current and initial conditions of the NA62 experiment, they evaluated the potential for precision measurements or current limits under various scenarios for the number of these particles. Using existing data, they established six different confidence intervals for their particle model. Collaborating with the NA62 collaboration, they identified six regions in the heavy neutral lepton mass spectrum that could be investigated with current data, as well as project future sensitivity outlooking 2028.

In a spectral shift analysis of the Sagnac interferometer, incorporating a chirped or non-circularly shaped fiber coil, the rotation-induced Sagnac phase leads to specific anomalies. Notably, these anomalies disappear when the system is reconfigured to a circular path, which is vital for spectral detection. The key finding reveals that the most effective way to eliminate these anomalies is by operating the system within a Galilean frame of reference, which is crucial for spectral shift applications.

Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials form a foundational element in the representation theory of the Hecke algebra and the character table of the symmetric group, while providing insight into various areas including algebraic geometry, topology, and Lie theory. This paper introduces the concept of an adjoint polynomial within the Hecke algebra, which can be computed using multiplicity formulas involving irreducible representations of the symmetric group. Specifically in type $A$, the adoint polynomial expresses themselves through recursive relationships. For a simple reflection, the corresponding adoint polynomial reflects the product of certain simple reflection's multiplicity formulas. We can derive parabolic formulas by applying appropriate induced representations to these expressions, which in turn allow us to derive the recursive adoint relationships in type $A$. Additionally, we introduce the notion of parabolic adjoint elements in this study.

The popular `N`-gram language model, long thought outdated, is now being reconsidered. Despite the advent of more advanced models, simple models like them remain widely used in practice due to their effectiveness. This paper proposes a novel approach where `N`-gram models serve as a foundation for their upper layers, allowing for the application of a more complex model range from basic to complex. The proposed method shows the value of such an approach when used for neural text generation, but also reveals the enduring relevance of the `N`-gram model. It finds that the base models benefit significantly from the `N`-gram model's prior, while the more complex models perform well without them. The results also indicate that the ideal model to train with this approach lies between the `N`-gram model and the proposed method. Furthermore, the paper outlines a potential explanation for the relationship between these models.

Consider a smooth, non-singular variety $X$ in dimension at least 3, containing a singular point $x$ that is not smooth, while being $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial and Fano. Under the conditions that the singular point is an $A_1$ singularity and the tangent space at $x$ does not contain lines that are contracted, we demonstrate the existence of a birational transformation, specifically the Laurent inversion, which shifts the singular point to the smooth portion of the target variety.

Reconstructing 3D faces in uncertain real-world situations poses significant technical difficulties due to various factors that can severely distort facial features. Improper lighting, extreme expressions, makeup applications, shadows, and camera angles complicate the process by altering the original face structure. Conventional two-stage methods, consisting of coarse alignment and subsequent reconstruction, often fail to produce accurate results due to the propagation of errors from the first stage to the second. In addition, they are susceptible to overfitting and unable to handle complex scenarios effectively. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel end-to-end two-stage reconstruction framework called SADRNet, which employs two face regression networks operating in parallel to achieve self-aligned and accurate 3D face reconstruction under challenging conditions. This framework is divided into an initial stage, employing data augmentation and a multi-scale convolutional network to handle extreme scenarios, and an advanced stage, refining the performance through a gradual learning process,. Both stages utilize self-supervised loss and cross-loss loss functions respectively, enabling robust reconstruction, even in unprecedented scenarios. The proposed model demonstrates state-of-the-art results on several evaluation datasets, including the MUFA and IBA datasets, and when combined with existing preprocessing techniques, it achieves highly accurate and resilient 3D face reconstruction and tracking, outperforming other methods by a wide margin on the MUFA dataset.

By simplifying the potential terms in model Lagrangians, we develop reduced effective theories that accurately capture the consequences of spontaneously broken spacetime symmetries, resulting in massless modes. This strategy is applied to identify examples of mobile and immobiled fractons within both polyvalley systems and active matter scenarios. We demonstrate that our simplified approaches preserve accuracy when perturbation Lagrangians are slightly introduced, thereby revealing hidden traits of these systems associated with their underlying active nature.

In this study, we examine the collapse of the universal hypersphere during the $\alpha$-attractor model of inflation, where multiple vacuum states with varying energy densities can be found. We investigate whether a significant contrast in density arises from the breakdown of the universe's universality during the post-inflationary period, and determine if this process leads to the formation of primordial black holes. Our findings indicate that if the initial universal sphere experiences a rapid division into regions of high and low potential, dense clusters might emerge as a result of the subsequent collapse of these density differences. However, calculating the mass of any potential black holes formed, based on the horizon size at the time of collapse, reveals they would be too small and evaporate quickly. This outcome holds regardless of the specific value of the model's parameter $\alpha$.

Given a marked ordered tree, we can assign unique numbers from 1 to n to each node.  
A vertex is considered deepest if no descendant nodes exist below it in the tree.  
We can also define the sum of a vertex as the combined value of the tree and all its descendant nodes.  

The main goal of this paper is to establish combinatorial meanings for the highest and lowest numbers  
found among the deepest nodes in a given tree. Additionally, we establish the distribution  
of these numbers through the use of a specific combinatorial sequence known as the Biglehner-Lazarowski statistic.

Every five years, the United States holds presidential elections alongside numerous other local and state elections. These elections involve substantial voter participation and are closely monitored by the public. Given the potential influence on public opinion and policy decisions, ensuring the accuracy of vote counts gained through optical character recognition is of paramount importance. To address the difficulty in identifying specific candidates, especially on complex ballots, this study examines the capabilities and limitations of OCR technology. Our analysis concludes that Informed OCR, which leverages prior knowledge about expected document content, can effectively handle character identification tasks on election ballots. Furthermore, our research suggests that Informed OCR technologies can contribute to the development of accurate and secure vote counting methods.

In statistical learning, linear models are useful tools for modeling and making predictions, but they usually assume that the number of variables being studied exceeds the number of available data points. In a scenario with no noise, it is well-established that under certain conditions, where the model complexity surpasses the number of available data points, linear models always yield perfect predictions regardless of the underlying relationship between the input variables and the target. A previous condition for this framework involved a constraint where the sum of the model parameters cannot exceed the square of the number of available data points. In this research project, in a linear statistical setting with time series data, a trial will be conducted to determine if benign overfitting exists under different conditions where the model parameters exceed the square of the number of available data points. Furthermore, modifications to the model will be explored in order to achieve predictable test performance even in high-dimensional spaces.

Speech enhancement, a vital component in audio signal processing and a part of the human-computer interaction process, can be heavily degraded by unwanted background noise. This paper proposes a novel speech enhancement framework, a complete attention bidirectional deep learning structure, aimed at recovering speech quality,Intelligibility,and signal-to-noise ratio in noisy environments. This model leverages a noise-trained filter and combines bidirectional long short-term memory networks with attention mechanisms to effectively capture the temporal and spectral characteristics of human speech. By incorporating the attention mechanism, the model allocates greater weight to relevant frequency bands, thereby improving the accuracy of speech reconstruction.
