Point clouds are often incomplete and noisy, which poses challenges for downstream tasks like training neural networks. Organizing them into structures (SSPs) can help, but a common issue arises: points from different parts of the shape may end up representing the same physical location, creating ambiguity. Existing methods use a loss function to minimize this organizational error, but since they don't penalize incorrect associations, they result in distorted and incomplete point clouds. We propose a novel approach called Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC) that initially sorts points by distance and then applies a global regularization to achieve a one-to-one correspondence. Our method produces high-quality SSPs from complex, closed shapes, which perform as well as or better than standard SSP generation techniques when used to train neural networks.

We're investigating multiple methods for multiple radar users to access a limited resource in an FMCW setup, which we model as a large system and evaluate various access patterns, including ALOHA and CSMA in discrete time, to find the most efficient distribution of a critical quantity. Our analysis reveals that ALOHA can't achieve the optimal distribution due to its non-myopic nature, but CSMA does a near-optimal job when there's sufficient access capacity. We also develop a simplified version of CSMA that does a second-best job. In the small system FMCW scenarios, we test actual CSMA protocols and modify them based on our theoretical insights, which the results show大幅 performance improvements near optimal.

Predicting the evolution of temporal knowledge graphs is an important task for a range of applications. This paper addresses this challenge by exploring a novel representation model that incorporates a flexible, low-rank structure. Our model enhances efficiency in both training and inference by leveraging a factorized form, which is also beneficial in terms of avoiding overfitting in scenarios with limited data. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on three real-world temporal knowledge graphs. Our results demonstrate significant performance improvements, outperforming both traditional and more recent methods by significant margins in hitting rate and outlier performance metrics. Furthermore, our work highlights the potential for transfer learning in scenarios where part of the temporal knowledge graph is unavailable, a characteristic found in many practical applications. Our findings also reveal remarkable reduction in parameters and increased efficiency in training and inference when compared to competing methods.

Within the Random Phase Approximation, the RPA is an extension of the Hartree-Fock method that accounts for weakly correlated many-body systems through the evaluation of slater determinants within the mean-field framework. In this study, we extend the HF-BRPA by incorporating short-range correlations via the Jost function method. By applying this method to the Root-Mean-Square Radius and Electric Dipole Giant Resonance of $^{16}$O, HF-BRPA and HF-RPA methods yield nearly the same results which both overestimate the experimental value of the EDR. Nonetheless, intriguingly, the BRPA method accurately predicts the $^{16}$O energy levels while outperforming both the HF-RPA and HF-RPA methods.

The prediction of extreme events in complex systems such as the climate is a challenging task. A newly proposed method allows for the identification of precursors to such extremes by analyzing time series data and dynamically determining relevant clustering approaches. This method selects a clustering technique that maximizes future event impact when applied to the data, enabling the creation of an impact-based state space representation. Once this representation is established, easily interpretable rules can be used to predict the occurrence of extreme values. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through prediction of values in a Lorenz attractor and climate-relevant variable in Earth's climate, as well as in the context of solar wind. Additional results are provided for a Rössler attractor and climate-relevant data from Mars.

Text generation models using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are being surpassed by Probabilistic Generative Models due to the difficulty of accurately modeling probability distributions with adversarial networks. As the training process forces the generator to create high-quality samples that deceive the discriminator, this results in a collapsed training process often seen in GANs. In contrast, limiting the training process to encode each target text into a sparse representation and differentiate only between real and fake samples by comparing it with random representations enables a stable training process. By reducing the dimensionality of the input data, a sparse code can capture the essential information while excluding unnecessary details, which is achieved by applying a sparse code encoder and the BERT base encoder to transform raw text. The training process is further aided by the use of an auxiliary predictor that takes the concatenation of the real text and the sparse code as input, which is called Spex. To directly model the sequence-to-sequence text generation process, we propose an alternative approach called Sparse GAN (Spagan). In this model, the generator encides each target text into a sparse representation, whereas the discriminant differentiates between real and fake sequences by comparing the predicted output of the auxiliary predictor. This allows the sparse representation to be meaningful while ensuring the collapse does not occur. The proposed model successfully outperforms the current state-of-the-art baselines in summarization and narrative generation tasks.

The hypothesis of extraterrestrial pansomia, which suggests life forms could be transferred between planets as they collide, has a theoretical basis but remains unproven scientifically. To explore this hypothesis, we developed a statistical model accounting for various factors including the transfer of organisms from one planet to another upon planetary impact, the organisms' ability to survive space travel, the frequency of interplanetary impacts, and the lifespan of planetary systems. Our analysis indicates that, on average, a solar system will exhibit signs of extraterrestrial pansomia for a certain duration, although significant variation exists between different systems. Our findings also highlight the importance of considering the habitable zone when assessing the feasibility of detecting extraterrestrial pansomia, suggesting it may be more prominent within these regions. Additionally, our research emphasizes the potential influence of large asteroids on the spread of life forms, suggesting they may serve as more resilient carriers compared to small particles, which could lead to increased cross-contamination and make detecting extraterrestrial pansomia more challenging.

We have developed a set of predictions using perturbation and "disturbance" theories for HI intensity mapping data obtained from interferometric observatories, taking into account the effects of large-scale structure on spatial distortions and the resulting impacts on power spectra and the subsequent biases in the parameters described by the Halofit model. Our theoretical predictions are particularly pertinent for the data that will be collected by the Low Frequency Array and the CHIME/CP2, and they are expected to significantly surpass the precision of current numerical simulations which struggle to accurately capture the effects of disturbance on dense Hi clouds within the redshift range 0.2-0.8. Moreover, we have explored the potential for intensity mapping datasets to provide new insights into the formation and disruption of these clouds, and the possible use of machine learning techniques to enhance the description of this phenomenon, in collaboration with the 21cm Fast Interferometric Survey. The ability to separate different components of Hi density using density power spectra and higher-order statistics is another development that could be leveraged to inform cosmological models and, ultimately, the application of intensity mapping data to the study of the lambda CDM model. We have identified specific features in the data that are most affected by cloud disruption and the potential for machine learning models to accurately capture the underlying patterns, in contrast to the limited accuracy of current simulation models.

We discover an interesting phenomenon in the Hubbard chain where the model undergoes an interesting process of spontaneous symmetry disruption that is accelerated by its neighbor in a chain of coupled hubs. As the inter-hub coupling decreases, there's a sudden surge in the rate of this disruption, revealing a cascading effect. noteworthy, we observe that this process spares certain quantities, such as local magnetization and charge gap, which merely experience an increase in magnitude. Furthermore, we find that the length of this process generally follows an exponential pattern with increasing chain length, although specific cases may exhibit more complex behavior.

Current spatial capture-recapture models don't effectively utilize pre-study resource selection information in analyzing movement and trapping data. A implicit alternative method was developed, which modifies traditional multi-state models by incorporating this information to create reduced state probabilities and thereby influence the positioning of virtual traps. A simulation study showed that explicitly integrating this information can decrease the need for data to track movement accurately. Furthermore, a case study using wild dogs in Namibia demonstrated the method's effectiveness, where the explicit model produced more precise estimates of population density than the implicit method or a conventional two-step method. The study indicated that utilizing this election method is particularly beneficial in studies involving animals with limited mobility and large home ranges, and it is recommended that researchers collect as much relevant prior information as possible.

In the Minimum Power k Edge Distinct st-Paths problem, the objective is to find k edge distinct paths between two vertices, s and t, in a given graph, such that the maximum edge weight among the paths is minimized. We have a notable advancement, being the first O(sqrt(k))-approximation algorithm for this problem, which can be achieved by a combination of techniques utilizing sparsification and rounding, building upon an existing O(log^2 k)-approximation algorithm. Notably, this approach yields an efficient 25-approximation algorithm for the scenario where k equals four.

This report examines the ability of an autonomous swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles to independently assess their surroundings based on their current position and the data they have received from a central planner and neighboring satellites. Each vehicle is capable of avoiding collisions by utilizing local sensing technology, such as a lidar, and by exchanging information about their positions and velocities with the swarm through a mesh communication network. The study demonstrates through both computer simulations and real-world testing that the swarm can successfully navigate through an environment and return to a designated base, even when some vehicles fail due to their reliance on data rather than direct sensory input.

To effectively combat the spread of network-based dynamic processes, understanding localization is crucial. While some research exists on this topic, it primarily focuses on tree structures and doesn't comprehensively examine the underlying mechanisms of the localization. This study aims to investigate network effect parameters on the spread of processes, using both analytical and numerical approaches. Our results show that the community structure significantly influences localization, allowing the process to spread widely within communities but hindering inter-community spread. In contrast, the random component has a limited impact on the localization even in highly connected networks. To quantify this effect, we introduce a localization coefficient that outperforms current methods in characterizing the spread. This coefficient can be applied to various network types and processes, providing a robust metric for assessing network modifications' potential to contain processes like viruses.

The author investigates the effectiveness of football defensive strategies by analyzing goal prevention techniques used by teams in recent UEFA EURO tournaments. To examine this, the study evaluates the impact of player positioning on defensive success, focusing on teams' average locations during crucial matches in UEFA EURO 2020 and 2022. By representing match situations as 3x3 grids, the researcher estimates the probability of a team avoiding defeat based on their player placement, taking into account home-field advantage. Comparing results from the two tournaments reveals consistent valuation methods, with certain locations proving more valuable than others, such as center-field versus boundary positions. Furthermore, the study finds similar outcomes for home and away games, with marginal differences reflecting the home-field advantage.

Modern mobile applications collect a lot of important user information.
The rate of these forms is increasing rapidly.
Giving users an easy time to fill out these forms is crucial, given their growing complexity.
We've designed a novel system called DVTFFR that identifies and extracts information from forms.
It operates without needing reference examples and identifies the fields automatically.
The architecture of DVTFFR uses a visual approach to locate, read, and organize the content without relying on text detection.
It also incorporates a unique organogram to map the hierarchical structure of form fields.
We tested our system's effectiveness through real-world experiments and found that it achieved an overall accuracy of 84.31% in extracting information.

Highly complex systems are frequently modeled using state-space models that allow for efficient analysis and prediction. These models are typically situated within a broader framework of dynamical systems theory, however, their application is often hindered by the need to linearize system dynamics, which results in inaccurate estimates, especially in non-linear systems. DTS-Space Models, a newly proposed class of state-space models, operate in the domain of dynamics and utilize latent variables to capture the hidden factors influencing system behavior. By describing the dynamics of these latent variables, we can obtain robust system estimates and insightful predictions. The model's utility has been validated in the control of a inverted pendulum, where its performance exceeded that of a conventional linear Kalman filter based controller.

Given an $N\times N$ Hermitian random matrix whose entries follow the semicircle distribution, the conditional freeness property has been established previously with respect to any sequence of deterministic unit trace matrices. In this study, we introduce a family of random matrices that includes the semicircle distribution as a special case, and prove the openness of type $B$ equates to conditional freeness for these matrices, particularly showing that the emm-monomial asymptotic freeness holds under these conditions. Furthermore, this work extends the scope of previous work by considering a broader class of matrices.

We study mappings from genus 1 curves to a genus 3 curve, specifically looking at the relationship between the Jacobians of these curves. The Jacobian of the genus 3 curve can be seen as the direct sum of the Jacobian of the genus 1 curve and another abelian surface, which we denote as Prym. We establish conditions under this equality and map out how the genus 1 curve's Jacobian relates to the Prym surface. Then, we give methods to find these relationships, providing an example in section 5.

In network analysis, identifying communities is often complicated by the presence of nodes not part of any community, known as structural polarization. Currently, there's limited research on normalizing the degree of polarization in networks, mainly due to the diverse formulas used in different methods, making comparison between the results difficult. To address this issue, we conducted a comprehensive study of several polarization measurement techniques, evaluating their properties and conducting polarization normalization to standardize a scale between zero and one. Our experiments revealed that conventional polarization measures struggle with detecting the degree of structural polarization, particularly in networks with high polarization. By introducing the concept of random polarization and conducting an evaluation of multiple measures, we discovered that most policies fail to accurately detect the degree of structural polarization. To address this issue, we proposed the RPA measure, which combines result and degree analysis of polarization and successfully normalizes the metric. Our tests showed that RPA outperforms other proposals in terms of polarizability detection and effective polarization scoring. Through the process of normalizing various polarization measures, we were able to provide a standardized framework for comparing the degree of structural polarization in networks.

The dynamics of multilayer networks can be divided into separate layers, 
each with its own unique interaction and correlated with the others through 
transmitted connections between nodes that span across different layers. Recent research has shown that 
transmitted interactions play a pivotal role in multiple domains including economics and neuroscience, by 
significantly influencing the behavior of individuals and time-consuming measurement techniques hamper 
comprehensively understanding multilayer systems. Our research presents an innovative approach to 
indirectly inferring transmission connections between oscillators within multilayer networks by analyzing 
how the networks' dynamics are linked across different layers. Our method pinpoints the essential 
transmitted connections that are responsible for producing similar behavior in multilayer networks and 
distinguishes itself from conventional clustering approaches in its ability to identify these connections 
accurately using a minimal amount of data as validated by numerical experiments on network models and 
real-world datasets. Our findings showcase the effectiveness of our model in an essential transmission 
sync game, highlighting the capacity of our method to improve performance when compared to alternative 
clustering approaches.

Given an open, flat region in space, we investigate the Cauchy stress operator as a function from three-dimensional space to the set of symmetric matrices. We seek the smallest set of independent functions that fully determine both the geometric and physical characteristics of a material, capable of accurately predicting its response to external forces. This minimum set comprises six functions that define the reference configuration, and materials with identical underlying structures are called isotropic. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for isotropic materials, the behavior of up to four-dimensional entities can be inferred by examining three-dimensional samples, due to maintained symmetry in their isotropy groups.

The significance of formal verification in programming depends on a program's ability to maintain a specified condition, but this only accounts for 50% of the task. Testing plays a crucial role in the remaining 50% by confirming that a program behaves as expected, yet this process is inherently unguided. Introducing a geometric testing approach, we aim to leverage the information about the desired program behavior provided in the form of code and comments to automatically generate and execute targeted scenarios. This process can be achieved using program slicing to create efficient testing programs, which can then be optimized using live data analysis and the removal of redundant operations. As a result, we obtain more precise and efficient scenarios that can be run at least 3 times faster than conventional test cases, providing more realistic program behavior and greater control over testing. This approach is demonstrated with a concrete example of sorting, where the desire for efficient sorting is expressed in the form of a program, which is then executed to generate and modify the testing scenario.

We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning through prompt-driven task embeddings. This method generates task-specific hyper-embeddings from textual prompts, which are then fed to a task-specific HyperNetwork. The resulting task embeddings can be incorporated into various layers of a Transformer model, effectively modifying its underlying task-conditioning. As HyperPrompt maintains its simplicity with hyper-embeddings as compact vectors and the potential for utilizing pre-trained models, it offers several advantages: the ability to control the efficiency of each targeted task using the length of hyper-embeddings; the modular addition of new tasks without necessitating the retraining of existing tasks; and the separation of data and model components. We demonstrate the versatility of HyperPrompt across diverse scenarios, including multi-task learning, few-shot learning, and hierarchical learning.

Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $B$ be the set of integers strictly less than $p$ and coprime to $p$. For any pair of vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ in the group $B \times B$, we define the function $N(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$ which counts the number of scalars $s$ such that the inner products $\langle \mathbf{a},s\mathbf{b}\rangle$ and $\langle \mathbf{b},s\mathbf{a}\rangle$ belong to the set $B$. By leveraging higher quadratic character sums, we establish an explicit formula for a substantial portion of prime numbers and an implicit bound for the remaining primes. Consequently, we derive a novel identity for primes of a specific form and obtain novel identities for certain lengths involving values of the Gauss $Q$-function and pairs of integers.

Quantum-dot excitation using long wavelengths generally results in poor, low-quality green light release, often biased towards a single color due to efficiency differences in the charge injection process. To address this issue, a new approach is proposed that involves pairing quantum dots with tunneling barriers on surfaces structured to preserve parity symmetry. This design enables symmetric charge release, leading to equal probabilities of emitting green and red light. A mathematical model and simulations back this concept, showing that a quantum dot structure with symmetric tunneling barriers can produce a quality green light close to an industry standard, along with parity protection enabling wide-angle light emission and green-red light quality close to each other. While our focus has been on quantum-dot light release, this innovative design may also benefit other applications involving quantum-dot packaging.

In the research community, there's a significant interest in understanding network scale without prior knowledge of the network's topological parameters. We propose a novel probabilistic network scale estimation algorithm that effectively resists Byzanine errors. Our implementation demonstrates the algorithm's efficiency by accurately determining the network diameter within 2x of the optimal value, while maintaining low latency and resource consumption.

</br>

To test the effectiveness of our algorithm in real-world scenarios, we created a hardware prototype using networked microcontrollers. Further, we conducted simulations on small-world networks to evaluate its performance under various conditions. Our research reveals that the estimated network scale grows exponentially with the network diameter and has a linear relationship with communication overhead.

</br>

In contrast to existing research, our work focuses on estimating the network scale in small-world networks without relying on a spanning tree, and provides robust scale estimates in the presence of Byzantine faults.

</br>

Our prototype and evaluation results show the feasibility and effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in real-world applications, outperforming existing approaches in terms of accuracy, latency, and resource consumption.

</br>

We made our implementation and results available at https://github.com/PrasannaV2/NSE_SW_Nodyze to encourage further research and development in the field.

</br>

We encourage existing small-world network researchers to consider using our network scale estimation algorithm in their experiments, and we appreciate any feedback on our approach.

</br

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study.

In numerical general relativity, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be satisfied by the chosen initial data. Our new method addresses this requirement for bondi coordinates, featuring a unique property: it automatically produces a conformally flat momentum constraint and sets the Hamiltonian constraint residual to zero under specific conditions. By formulating the problem as a Poisson equation, we can leverage standard, high-order, boundary-respecting solution techniques, including the spectral method. Numerical experiments demonstrate that, as the resolution increases, the Hamiltonian constraint residual converges to zero, indicating our method's effectiveness.

The search for rare decay processes in the Sigma plus baryon sector has been conducted using the LHCb data, specifically in the dilectron channel. Analytical results displayed on a mass spectrum strongly indicate the existence of a new decay mode for the Sigma plus baryon, with an anomaly appearing at a specific mass threshold. The calculated parameters of this anomaly are in agreement with simulated expectations for the newly discovered process. However, additional verification is needed to determine whether this finding is a statistical artifact or a genuine discovery.

We report an unusually large Lonzato effect observed in antiferromagnetic
Mn$_3$NiN, which reaches values between 20 and 80 $\mu$V T$^{-1}$ kB$^{-1}$
(kOmega cm)$^{-1}$. The in-plane resistivity and Nernst signal exhibited a
distinctive nonlinear relationship, suggestive of significant contributions
from the Hall signal. The dependence of the Nernst signal on the magnetic
field displayed asymmetry characteristic of the anomalous Hall signal.
Measurements performed with the sample normal aligned along the q-axis of
Mn$_3$NiN revealed the onset of the Hall signal at the Néel temperature,
whereas alignment along the gamma axis showed the onset at the Curie point.
The shape of the Nernst signal changed when the sample normal was aligned
along the gamma axis compared to the q-axis, indicating that different
magnetic sublattices are probed in these two scenarios.

Although training deep neural networks by experts in few areas is feasible, it becomes challenging when applying to broader field training due to the limited number of specialists. To overcome this limitation, research has focused on training models via a single instructor but becomes more complicated when multiple instructors are involved. We propose a novel approach called PILE, Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble, that enables training from numerous instructors on a large data scale and ranks among the top methods on the Google Search dataset. PILE processes wide field training in two stages: first, it narrows the training scope into localized regions where a single instructor can effectively guide the model. Next, it iteratively adds training regions guided by new instructors, using an ensemble of models to guide each sub-region in subsequent stages. Experiments show that PILE achieves exceptional performance in wide field training, outperforming current multi-instructor techniques and yielding consistent results when a single instructor is involved.
This lecture will address both beam dynamics and beam reductions in circular accelerators, utilizing established resources from previous lectures by R. Tomas and R. Tomas.

The availability of synchrotron radiation and x-rays from user facilities has enabled researchers to obtain crucial insights into materials, leading to rapid progress across multiple disciplines. To take advantage of these facilities, users employ various experimental techniques, from imaging to spectroscopy, often combining them in complex approaches. Given the time-consuming and highly specialized nature of these experiments, users require access to intuitive, powerful, and user-friendly interfaces that provide real-time access to data and expert knowledge. This can be achieved by integrating specialized software tools into the control systems of user facilities, allowing for intelligent control, visualisation, and effective resource management by both on-site staff and visiting researchers. This integration can be facilitated by linking the control systems to artificial intelligence/enabling technologies through the use of the Eclipse Theia framework, which has already established connections with established software tools and is established across multiple domains.

We establish regularity properties of the boundary between obstacle and free space, as well as associated gradient behaviors, for solutions to a specific non-autonomous obstacle problem governed by sub-quadratic growth conditions. Specifically, the Dirichlet variant of the heat equation and its more general parabolic settings with divergent coefficients can be derived from our results.

This work explores the impact of temperature anisotropy on geodesic acoustic modes in a plasma where T_parallel exceeds T_perpendicular. The presence of magnetic field line bending causes energy and angular momentum transfer, which can either damp or enhance plasma oscillations depending on the ratio of perpendicular to parallel temperatures. For significant temperature anisotropy, Gaussian geometry can lead to growth of oscillations, potentially surpassing the threshold for geodesic acoustic mode instability.

Quantum annealing has been widely employed in both hardware and software to solve combinatorial optimization problems, particularly those involving non-stoquastic annealing engines. Unlike standard stoquastic annealing, non-stoquastic Hamiltonians do not allow the ground state to be directly reached, thus, previous studies have largely focused on finding "sweet spots" to minimize the impact of unwanted excited states. In this study, we challenge this perspective and suggest that the ground state is not necessarily the most highly populated state as a consequence of quantum decoherence, enabling QA systems equipped with non-stoquastic annealers to efficiently function. Furthermore, we demonstrate theoretically and support this claim through numerical simulations and real hardware experiments, showing that, given sufficient decoherence, both stoquastic and non-stoquastic quantum annealing can be_quenched_ to achieve high ground state fidelity. Our empirical evidence suggests that QA utilizing a Hamiltonian featuring a transverse field three-spin interaction outperforms both stoquastic Hamiltonians, typically exhibiting a 10% higher ground state fidelity in practical applications. These observations imply that, rather than being hindered by non-stoquastic interactions, QA systems can leverage them to achieve optimal performance.

This essay explores the background of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, his role in establishing the Cape Astronomical Laboratory under the direction of Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn, and his involvement in creating the innovative method of the Selected Areas Scheme for the cataloging of southern stars.

This paper proposes a novel approach to defining Serre weights for GL_2 over K3 fields, eschewing mu_filtration in favor of employing local Artin representations. By leveraging K3 fields' properties, we derive a crucial connection between a K3 field's extension and its n-tuple local Artin representations, which enables us to establish the existence and semi-simplicity of certain filtrations. These developments facilitate an exploration of weight type questions for ordinary eigenforms, allowing us to prove the prevalence of clear weights among these eigenforms and provide a deeper understanding of their distribution.

We establish that in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, sequences of compact, smoothly bounded hypersurfaces with limited mean curvature and uniform volume and area properties converge in the Blaschke sense to the directable limit in the sense of measures, together with isoperimetric residues in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\times\mathbb{R}$; this result holds for directed variations. This finding provides a novel mesoscale regularity condition for families of hypersurfaces and enables a more in-depth investigation of directed convergence, particularly near singularities, to reveal detailed structural information about specific surface families. This research builds upon and expands upon the work of Reshetnyak and St. Peter.

A recent deep neural network (DNN) inference acceleration technique involves using multiple independent critics who evaluate specific regions of the input space and train separately to minimize their respective error rates. While effective for single-machine learning, this approach faces challenges when applying it to deep DNNs learned in a model-parallel manner, due to the requirement of retraining each critic after others fail. To overcome this, we propose a novel strategy where each critic focuses on a specific region and is trained using data that minimizes its region's expected value. This allows for model-parallel training and inference of multiple independent critics. We then demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in training a 22-layer DNN for the SVHN dataset, achieving a validation accuracy of 97.42% with two critics, and 97.41% with one critic.

Advanced composite materials are typically designed to include self-sensing technology that integrates pressure and damage detection into the final product, reducing the need for additional external components and complex integration processes. However, a challenge arises when certain events, like pressure applied to a material, cause unintended damage, compromising the integrity of the self-sensing system. This research paper presents an innovative approach to address this issue by utilizing electrical impedance tomography and a genetic algorithm to create a routing structure that precisely prevents desired damage at a specific location, such as at a puncture point, while allowing other damage to occur in response to an outside stimulus. Demonstration of the concept is achieved through a multi-phase pressure experiment, showing that external stress induces damage in an unpredictable pattern, rendering it impossible for traditional self-sensing techniques to accurately measure internal stress. By implementing the proposed genetic algorithm and impedance tomography method, a specific damage distribution is accurately produced when applying external pressure to a material, illustrating a novel and effective method for materials with built-in self-sensing capabilities.

We've examined a previously discussed argument, which claimed that hierarchy arises from intelligent entities overcoming less capable ones, resulting in the more competent occupying the top of the structure. However, we contend that the definition of intelligence employed was ambiguous. Therefore, we've explored this concept through three distinct lenses, each yielding a different outcome. Using an overwhelming force to surpass a weaker element to assume a position above it, as suggested in the original argument, we've discovered that according to the current understanding of general intelligence, hierarchy would indeed emerge. Alternatively, we've found that a different type of superiority could lead to the collective group of autonomous agents displaying a more sophisticated understanding than any individual agent. Moreover, we've found that when examining intelligence from the perspective of adaptability, the interaction between the entities would lead to the development of a diverse set of specialized skills that would benefit the entire system.

In this scenario, a significant alternative to measurements, in this case, a general direction, is available for each decision, although it has limited influence on the system's state. In a discrete state space, we prove that optimal policies can be derived from a minimal set of measurements, specifically no more than $|S|/|D|$, in combination with the available alternative, in this case, a significant proportion $|S|/|D|$, in this case, a significant proportion. In addition, we offer a novel method to infer the ideal policy from these elements, which allows it to adapt seamlessly to any situation, regardless of the specific measure taken, in this case, a significant measure, in this case, a significant proportion, in this case, a significant proportion. This study explores a new tensor framework for describing the geometry of Euclidean spaces, centered on a fresh interpretation of the rotation tensor in relation to geometric quantities such as angular velocity, angular acceleration, angular momentum, and angular momentum rate of change. These elements are key to formulating the equations of angular motion. The discussion builds on existing literature, referencing works by Y. Peres, M. Kutzback, A. Kolesnik, and H. Cholewa & J. Tounda.

Certain theoretical models suggest certain particles could change flavor and be very light, yet currently, experimental data on flavor-changing neutral currents are very restrictive. To address this issue, researchers have proposed the idea of long-lived photons that emit delayed radiation. This allows for the possibility of visible tracks in experiments and even projectable direct detection in future projects like FASER$\nu$ and CTAEPC. This concept holds promise for discovering new particles at the LHC and beyond. 

Our research focuses on extending the Constrained Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model with a singlet and exploring the possibility of visible electrons emitting photons in this model. Through theoretical calculations and the use of established tools, we have analyzed all possible two-body and three-body decays of the electron in this model. By applying constraints and choosing specific parameters, we have been able to simulate the trajectories of photons in the ATLAS detector at high energies. 

Overall, our results show that specific decay channels of the electron could result in observable long-lived photons within the ATLAS detector at high energies. This finding also motivates further investigation into related models and the possibility of precise simulations of photon emission in future projects like FASER$\nu$ and CTAEPC.

The sudden shift to remote learning imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the intended learning experiences for both educators and students. This shift forced them to adapt to remote instruction and learning, which required them to overcome technical, physical, and psychological barriers caused by the pandemic. This adaptation led to varying levels of preparedness for remote learning among students, ultimately influencing their ability to keep up with the curriculum. A survey was conducted with university students in the United States to gather data on their ability to stay on track during remote learning. This study found that students' cognitive processes were significantly impacted by technical and physical barriers and necessary adaptations in response to physical challenges, with non-significant impacts arising from psychological barriers. Structural equation modeling was used to analyze the data, with all criteria for both confirmatory and exploratory analyses met.

We demonstrate that the global symmetry of the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda conformal field theory can be expanded to include rotations and translations, modifying the standard Conze-Iwaniec identity. This modification enables us to establish an $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ equivalent of the Merenlak inequality. Furthermore, this new framework enables a rigorous, measure-theoretic proof of the absence of discrete series within certain Borel subsets of the positive real line, which was previously proven using unitary representation theory alone. Additionally, this revised approach provides a measure-theoretic proof of the density of primary fields in certain subfamilies of the Liouville unitary CFT.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups belong to the class of bi-automatic groups,
implying they are also of type $FP_2$, and have a binary presentation. As
consequences, we derive that finite reflection groups in various domains, including
$Cox(n)$, $Aff(n)$, and $Aff^+(n)$, are both bi-automatic and of type $FP_2$.

We investigated the thermodynamics and law conservation of a charged AdS black hole in the presence of a scalar field, both numerically and analytically. Our study revealed that the maximum charge of the black hole is determined by its thermodynamic stability and occurs at an extremal state, confirming the validity of the cosmic censorship conjecture. Furthermore, we discovered that perturbations of the maximum charge in charged AdS black holes can expose their singularities. Interestingly, we found that all such black holes exhibit a maximum charge beyond which their singularities would be exposed, regardless of the scalar field's charge coupling parameter. Moreover, the value of this parameter significantly affects the allowable range of perturbations. When the parameter is less than two, we demonstrated that a charged Reissner-Nordstr$\ddot{o}$m black hole in an asymptotically flat spacetime can violate the cosmic censorship conjecture by exposing its singularity through a perturbation of its charge in response to a perturbation of its scalar field near its extremal horizon.

In this research, we adapt the classical ZFC axioms to a set of alternative logical systems that include paraconsistent and paracomplete logics, specifically adjusting the underlying classical two-valued logic to more complex logical systems. Notably, our work demonstrates the feasibility of a paraconsistent version of ZFC, utilizing the paraconsistent logic $n$-VAL with more than two classical values, modifying the ZFC axiom of collection to accommodate this new logical framework. Furthermore, our collection axiom enables the establishment of a theory equivalent to the classical ZFC under the standard interpretation. Additionally, our feasibility analysis extends to a range of other paraconsistent and paracomplete versions of ZFC, each featuring distinct characteristics in their truth tables and logical behaviors.

Recent discoveries have classified quiescent locomotor patterns into stationary, 'walking', and low-amplitude types. Although the static walking states have been well-documented, their distinct dynamic characteristics remain unclear. This research investigates whether specific step frequencies can be identified within these dynamic quiescent states. Data was gathered from an implantable electrocorticogram device placed on the motor cortex of three freely moving rats' heads. Time series analysis techniques, encompassing recurrence network theory and topological persistent homology, were adapted for use with noisy data to extract meaningful insights. Findings showed that distinct structural properties of recurrence networks and point clouds corresponded to each of the three quiescent locomotor states, with particularly pronounced differences identified during low-amplitude walks. Furthermore, a specific metric known as the clustering coefficient displayed variations over time that aligned with the walking states and distinguished them from the stationary states, using a significant threshold. These results suggest that both short and long-range correlations in brain activity play a critical role in defining distinct patterns of low-amplitude walking brains.

This calculation calculates the entropy of any probability distribution by leveraging a connection between entropy and the log-nested sequence produced by nested sampling. Our method has potential advantages over conventional entropy estimation techniques, as it allows for approximate calculation of the Kullback-Leibler entropy within the log-nested sequence, which decreases monotonically, making it particularly useful for high-dimensional parameter spaces (d > 10), where it avoids the necessity of sampling, and it can be efficiently applied to time-series data, allowing for dimensionality reduction (d < 10), where it benefits from combining with established nested sampling estimator methods.

We examine right-angled Artin complexes, focusing on their non-trivial splitable isomorphisms by removing a specific vertex from the associated graph. Under the condition that the complex contains a contractible tree-like structure, we can find a vertex whose removal results in two smaller complexes that are also tree-like. This finding is a key technical component in the underlying research. Using this result, we can show that if a complex has a splitable isomorphism, it must contain a specific element called a stable map. This proof makes significant progress towards a long-standing conjecture and allows us to derive a right-angled version of a previously proven theorem.

In the field of neuroscience, connecting brain activity patterns is crucial for comprehending both normal brain function and pathologies affecting the brain. Structural connectivity maps the brain's static structural connections via imaging, while functional connectivity identifies active connections from brain activity using various imaging techniques. However, treating functional connectivity as dynamic is essential, given the brain's active nature, but current methods face efficiency challenges due to high computational demands and difficulties in modeling the highly sparse nature of brain connections. To tackle these issues, we introduce a novel deep learning approach that utilizes a matrix-factorized variant of the Kroencke graph eta representation and a suitable reparametrization to enable probabilistic inference, thereby obtaining dynamic efficient connectivity (DEC) estimates directly from simultaneous electroencephalogram and functional magnetic resonance imaging data. Our method, DECNet, outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in accurately predicting seizures and classifying patients' cognitive states, demonstrating the potential of efficient connectivity representation in providing an optimal balance between descriptive capacity and interpretability.

The networks we use to model evolutionary histories vary in complexity from simple tree structures to highly detailed phylogenetic networks that incorporate phenomena such as hybridization and lateral gene transfer. Since the discovery of these more complex events, researchers have investigated how they might influence evolutionary processes by examining events in space and time through statistical tools. Despite this progress, there is a gap in our knowledge regarding the effects of different types of network structures on event frequencies. This research fills that gap by exploring how various network designs affect the occurrence of specific events, using a range of design methods. Ultimately, it reveals that certain structures, unlike others, can lead to higher or lower rates of specific events, with implications for choosing the right network models.

Determining whether a sample contains active, living organisms is a common laboratory test called the viability assay.  As video microscopy becomes the standard method for observing cells and microorganisms, there's also an increased need for automated analysis through computational systems that can identify biological movement in video samples.  In this project, we developed a simple yet effective algorithm to detect biological movement in video by combining visual features and data from slow motion videos, generated via microscopy, to create an accurate automated classification system. Our approach uses a simple yet effective algorithm to achieve high accuracy in detecting biological movement in video samples.

In various scientific disciplines, resolving linear systems often necessitates inverting a matrix, a labor-intensive and resource-draining process for large-scale problems. By leveraging fast iterative matrix inversion techniques, we can substantially reduce computation time, particularly when dealing with a vast number of related linear systems sharing the same matrix. Utilizing higher-order methods such as Neumann series and Landau-Davis series on diagonalizable matrices dramatically accelerates this process in GPU-accelerated environments. We have expanded upon the Neumann and Landau-Davis series in our research paper and demonstrated significant reductions in computation time - up to 7 times faster - compared to traditional GPU-inversion algorithms or successive approximations.

This paper develops a rigorous framework for analyzing the average energy deposition as a function of energy for waves scattered by various objects, across both non-relativistic and relativistic contexts. Our approach employs a perturbation theory, specifically using small time increments to determine the scattering system's response to a wave with a broad spectrum of frequencies or energies. We derive a general formula for the integral of the deposition probability and demonstrate its applicability through detailed calculations in both non-relativistic and relativistic scenarios, including non-quantum electrodynamic settings. Our examples illustrate the dependence of deposition on frequency or energy in different scenarios and confirm our calculations with experimental data.

We provide an analytical framework to examine the three-dimensional topological Ando conductor within a cubic lattice, in the presence of random discontinuous disorders. Our model is then simplified by randomly applying binary disorders within the lattice. Using large-N approximations, we derive key STS features associated with both binary and multi-gaussian disorder scenarios, both theoretically and through numerical simulations. Our results show that in a large-N scenario, the characteristic energy gap vanishes in a second-order phase transition, which can be accurately predicted by our disordered SSH model. Additionally, we observe an intrinsic bi-faciality within the STS spectra of the 3D TI, arising from the directional asymmetry in spatial energy levels. This asymmetry leads to the local real-space electron distribution exhibiting topological inertial properties.

The concept of linear cutting has been extensively studied in the framework of vector spaces since the pioneering work of Hadwiger and Mader, but extending this study to more complex linear structures presented numerous challenges. In this article, we introduce the foundational elements of a linear cut theory for quiver spaces, establishing a fresh perspective on these structures and their relationship to linear cuts. Our approach demonstrates how linear cuts can be understood as maximal compactness within subunits of quiver spaces, leveraging their ability to preserve certain algebraic properties under the Kunneth functor. This property enables combining independent linear cuts into combined units, and it is this aspect that sets quiver spaces apart from more basic algebraic structures like groups or modules.

We examine a particular scenario within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, where the mu parameter is set equal to the product of the MSSM mu parameter and the on-shell Higgs boson mass. In this scenario, the on-shell Higgs becomes a physical particle. However, if the bilinear term in the superpotential has a phase of pi/2, the on-shell Higgs acquires a purely imaginary value. On the other hand, if the mu term has the same phase, the on-shell Higgs gains non-zero couplings to two other physical scalars in the model, specifically the complex CP-even Higgs and the charged Higgs. Given that the on-shell Higgs would interact with standard model particles, we investigate the implications of this on the current and future experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider.

A new statistic has been developed to test linearity in a generalized model that encompasses an arbitrary structure of the network and varies across observations. The proposed method is robust and remains consistent under both smooth and sharp alternatives, a property rare in the field of nonparametric statistics. When adapted to the case of a random network, the statistic can be evaluated using the Monte Carlo method to derive suitable critical values. This adaptation enables the creation of a more accurate linearity threshold, a first of its kind in the field of econometrics. A simulation study and empirical analysis have been conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method.

Recent research has introduced the concept of Deep Declarative Networks (DDNs), which combines graph-based learning methods and gradient backpropagation to create novel, framework-specific representations of traditional machine learning problems. This innovation has led to the development of improvements in a variety of fields, from graph learning to matrix factorization and set selection. A key limitation of DDNs is that the constraints within each framework restrict the applicability and interpretability of the results, thereby hindering potential performance gains. To address this limitation, we propose expanding the DDNs architecture by introducing a more flexible set of declarative constraints within a specific problem framework. We focus on two, closely related problems, isotonic regression and network design, and propose the generalized DDNs (GDDNs) to enable more effective backward propagation while maintaining the benefits of the original framework. Our results indicate that GDDNs outperforms both the original DDNs and conventional alternatives in a variety of benchmark evaluations, as presented while preserving the unique advantages of the two problem frameworks.

A cell's interaction with its surroundings is influenced by the fact that it is enclosed by a membrane. This causes certain flow fields that may relocate proteins within the membrane through a process known as tangential advection. This process must be considered in cell-based models because it can influence how proteins aggregate and migrate, especially when the cell disperses. In contrast, typically cell-based models focus on a cell's motility but disregard how the membrane and attached proteins respond to the cell's movement. Instead, these models usually employ strong assumptions to avoid dispersional effects or control the distribution of proteins. To address this limitation, the recent research introduces a new cell-dispersal and motility model without making arbitrary assumptions to ensure the reliable aggregation of proteins. This framework is designed to efficiently and accurately capture the behavior of proteins within proteins that are subject to the cell's interaction with its surroundings.

The primary function of a blockchain is to enable the secure transfer of assets between parties. However, this purpose can be exploited by bad actors who seek to hide the source and destination of transferred currency by creating complex transaction patterns, also known as mixing. These actors try to remove metadata from the blockchain and rely on automatic analysis tools for currency tracing, which can lead to inaccurate interpretations when ignoring the actual data and transaction history. As new cryptocurrencies emerge, incorporating features for privacy and security directly into the blockchain, including encryption and consensus mechanisms, poses a significant threat to traditional tracing methods and underscores the need for more effective anti-money laundering strategies in response to evolving cryptocurrency technologies.

This research proposes using reinforcement learning to create robust, fault-tolerant quantum computations without requiring precise timing in tolerance schemes. We simplify the learning process for by-Lazy encoding, a specific error correction method. To test our approach, we simulated learning occurrences for faults that the QRAC cannot normally handle. The results showed the QRAC and the modified by-Lazy encoding both successfully maintained a fault-correcting capability of one quantum bit of information. Furthermore, the by-Lazy encoding could be taught to manage two simultaneous errors involving erasure, assuming the errors were at least two lattice spacings apart.

In the quantum leap metrology scheme, superposing coherent states leads to a notable, easily measurable change in average photon numbers at specific times during a Rabi oscillation. We analyze the precision with which an unknown parameter can be measured through this process within a two-coupled cavity system, where we also investigate the influence of cavity coupling and initial state on the measurement's success. Our simulations, considering various forms of noise, demonstrate that this approach effectively achieves Heisenberg-like precision scaling, particularly in the presence of erasure losses.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron associations in 200 GeV/A $d$+$Au$ and $Au$+$Au$ collisions. These collisions include measurements of associated hadron distributionst, which are categorized by $z$ (hadron longitudinal momentum fraction) and $p_T$ (transverse momentum). Notably, $d$+$Au$ collisions exhibit an average hadron increase of 170% above nuclear deep inelastic scattering functions, whereas $Au$+$Au$ collisions exhibit an associated hadron increase of 170% above nuclear deep inelastic scattering functions. These collisions collide at a velocity of $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV.

This paper extends the basic Smarandache's digit multiplication concept to encompass any given function applied to individual digits. We specifically address the 'smarandache's sigma multiplication' of digits, which involves the sigma of applied functions to each digit. We then derive general properties and formulas regarding this topic.

Network noise and network-induced randomness are crucial considerations when designing network systems. Network capacity is typically measured using Goodput, which represents the net data transferred from source to destination after accounting for protocol overhead. This paper delves into the scalability limits of networked systems and provides an analytical model for noise in the clouds. The proposed model, characterized by stochastic fluctuations in network connectivity and variability in data transfer times, enables scalability analysis of cloud networks. Two key parameters of the model are explored to reveal the network's influence on system scalability. The results indicate that high variability in network connectivity and data transfer times can lead to reduced scalability, whereas low noise levels can promote increased system performance. The proposed model is validated through numerical simulations and real-world measurements, leveraging the NS-3 network simulator and cloud benchmarking tools.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with numerous applications and has been extensively studied. We investigate a scenario where many learners participate in the same contextual linear bandit setting but communicate minimally. These learners do not exchange extensive information and do not need to be aware of the number of others involved. Our first main contribution is the development of a learning algorithm for this scenario, which we call Single Augmented Policy (SAP). This algorithm achieves an accumulated regret close to the optimal level, equivalent to $T^{4/5}$ times the accumulated regret of a contextual linear bandit learning setting. Moreover, the algorithm requires very little communication, amounting to only $o(T)$ per setting. Moreover, the algorithm achieves the same sample complexity and context dimension dependence as contextual linear bandit learning. Our second main contribution is an adaptive version of the algorithm, called Multi-Augmented Policy (MAP). This algorithm achieves the same accumulated regret equivalence as the basic algorithm but exhibits the same performance in the worst-case scenario. MAP's regret equals $\T^{4/5}$ times the optimal regret of a contextual linear linear bandit learning setting and exhibits the same accumulated regret equivalence in non-stochastic and stochastic settings. These results indicate that contextual linear bandit learning agents can communicate very little while still performing close to the optimal level. The results also indicate that adding a very small amount of information and context to the basic single learning context does not significantly increase the accumulated regret.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading to the adaptation of Agile methodologies, particularly Scrum, to accommodate collaborative efforts from remotely based teams. However, the implementation of Scrum from home poses several challenges that could undermine team performance and the overall project's success. Our research aims to examine the effects of remote working on Scrum project outcomes and the crucial role it plays in enabling team success. Through a multi-method approach, we collected data from three distinct sources: initial expert opinions, real-world working professionals using Scrum, and empirical support from over 300 web applications developed using the methodology. Our findings indicate that remote working hinders the direct contribution of Scrum to web application development projects, but this can be mitigated by enhancing communication capabilities within teams. Moreover, our results suggest that teams utilizing Scrum achieve higher levels of project success when they leverage their communication abilities to overcome the challenges posed by remote working.

We appreciate the interest shown by readers from the University of Michigan, Ohio State University, and Purdue University. Their input, particularly the comments from Professor Liang and their team, significantly influenced our decision to incorporate the evolutionary strategy suggested in theirJO into our primary publication's version of record. Furthermore, our initial findings were sparked by an oral presentation at the University of Michigan, further validated by positive feedback from colleagues during the presentation.

This study investigates the use of event shape engineering to explore the connection between fluid dynamics and the overall lead-ion collision dynamics. By selecting specific events based on the dilectron pair's elliptic flow coefficient, measured with the ALICE detector at the ALICE experiment during the 2015 Pb-Pb collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, we observed that the average transverse momentum depends on the chosen selection of dimuon pairs. A comparable result was found in the 2013 Pb-Pb collisions at the same energy. Literature indicates that this dependency can be accounted for by considering the initial geometry and the initial entropy distribution. Consequently, the event shape engineering technique reveals that complex dynamical processes can be simplified, making it more accessible to the influence of higher-order effects.

This lecture introduces the basics of quaternion algebra and analysis, focusing on Euler-Newton functions and providing a brief overview of the LCTS. It then defines the quaternion LCTS and discusses its fundamental properties before examining various types of uncertainty principles associated with it.

This research investigates the extremal GDoF advantage of optimal power control over a binary power control method, utilizing BPSK modulated signals, and discovers the benefit scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ for networks with $K$ users. In contrast, peripheral network regions exhibit a marginal $\Theta(\log^{1/2} K)$ advantage, thereby demonstrating that the vast majority of significant gain arises within the extremal conditions.

This research focuses on particle-resolved direct numerical simulation (DRDNS) of turbulent multiphase flows, and addresses the issue of collision frequency in DRDNS at high solid-to-fluid density ratios ($\phi\rho_{p}/\rho$). As increasing this ratio decreases the collision frequency in DRDNS, users may encounter difficulties due to excessive computational costs necessitated by more frequent collisions. We propose implementing a multiple time step (MTS) integration technique for the particle phase in DRDNS. However, applying standard MTS methods is problematic as they assume infinite collisons at high solid-to-fluid density ratios. To address this challenge, we introduce an MTS approach that incorporates finite collisions in its framework. We further present a newly developed algorithm combining this MTS method with the contact list update in DRDNS. showcase the algorithms performance through post-processing step size increases of 10^1.5 and 10^2 times in a well-documented DRDNS case, and demonstrate the MTS method's capability to achieve the same physical collision time with reduced computational cost as the single time step (STS) method, but with larger post-processing steps, when solid-to-fluid density ratio is sufficiently high, despite needing further verification for lower solid-to-fluid density ratios.

This article offers an infinite sequence of whole number solutions to the equation
$a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ (for non-negative integer $n$), by establishing a basis for infinitely many integer solutions to this Diophantine equation.
We derive a sequence of whole number solutions to the equation, verify its validity for all values of $n$, and provide an analytical derivation of its correctness.
Additionally, this analysis is linked to a more general research area, specifically examining which prime numbers $p$ allow integer solutions to the equation
$a^2+ab+b^2=p^n$.

This paper presents the development of a simple one-legged hopping robot capable of moving through a soft surface. We utilized a mathematical model to simulate the robot's movement through varying levels of soil firmness. To validate the model, we built and tested the physical robot, confirming its performance through experimental data. Additionally, we proposed an improved control method using a hybrid approach, combining two existing control techniques. The results demonstrated that the robot's hopping distance could be significantly increased by switching from one control method to another at a specific moment. The robot's operation, validated by a 3D animation, aids in designing efficient single-legged hopping robots.

We introduce a comprehensive flexible model, encompassing the whole meson momentum range, built upon the Bjorken variable and adhering to fundamental constraints. This formulation unifies diverse flexible parametrisations such as the Bjorken, Georgi-Polchinski, Leutwyler-Sterman and HQET forms factors. Furthermore, it can be employed to describe meson production processes via photon-proton collisions, such as vector meson production at HERA. A detailed comparison of our new flexible parametrisation for the whole momentum range with existing data and the previously mentioned schemes has been performed for the ground state mesons, including $\pi$, $\eta$, $\eta'$ and vector meson ($\rho$, $\omega$, $\phi$, $J/\psi$ and $\U$) by means of the Gounaris-Sakurai model, the Bourrely-Cohen-Lévy and light cone sum rule approaches.

In this work, we examined the less understood effects in the droplet electrohydrodynamic mode, particularly how airflows impact the droplet by examining its result on the droplet itself. A notable observation occurred when a droplet subjected to a high-voltage field broke down and formed a surface layer of charged droplets, creating an "EHD fan" that emitted smaller droplets and formed a balanced system. Furthermore, we observed the formation of counter-rotating vortices within the main droplet caused by the fan's EHD forces, which ultimately led to mixed flows and efficient mixing of fluids. However, the droplet itself experienced less deformation due to the EHD forces exerted by the fan, demonstrating a notable demonstration of the delicate interaction between high-voltage fields and moving droplets. Ultimately, this research provides a compact platform for studying droplet dynamics and may have implications for improving processes in the chemical and biotechnological industries as well as for understanding the behavior of fat cells in milk.

Effectively handling negation is a significant hurdle in creating intelligent systems able to interpret natural language. 
To tackle complex problems involving negation, systems must understand both simple concepts, like "not taking medication," and deeper, more abstract notions, such as the impact of a treatment when a patient does not take the medication. 
To evaluate the ability of current models to grasp negation, we have assembled a diverse set of 1,000 sentences covering various domains and types of relationships, based on existing datasets. 
We then conducted an in-depth assessment of existing approaches before introducing a new training regimen that utilizes pre-trained language models to alleviate the influence of semantic understanding. 
Our results show that models trained on our carefully curated dataset consistently outperform those trained on the current standard benchmarks across all models and network sizes tested.

Comprehending the structural hierarchies of complex networks is crucial for
congestion management, effective resource allocation, and the optimization of
restoration procedures following natural disasters. While numerous methods exist
to quantify hierarchies in complex networks, there is a significant gap in the
development of efficient and scalable frameworks that can compute and visualize
these hierarchical patterns. In this study, we present a comprehensive framework
for representing and visualizing the inherent hierarchies within information
networks, with a focus on mitigating congestion through effective routing. This
framework integrates and augments existing concepts, including centripetal
forces, potential hierarchies, and clustering coefficients, to produce a robust
and interpretable hierarchical structure. Our approach enables the efficient
computation of cluster coefficients at any level of a hierarchy's branch, thereby
demonstrating its potential to accurately reflect the inherent hierarchies
observed in networks. By utilizing our framework, we can effectively compare
and visualize clustering coefficients across different parts of a network's
hypothetical hierarchy, with applications ranging from the internet to online
social networks and the world wide web. This leads to the identification of a
characteristic curve that exhibits distinct scaling patterns, crucial for the
effective design of information flows in complex networks. To further enhance
this framework's functionality, we introduce a novel approach to visualize the
world wide web's hierarchical structure, effectively illustrating its complex
organizational patterns.

Quantum annealing is a method that can efficiently solve a vast number of optimization problems with minimal computation time, especially when dealing large-scale, randomly generated inputs.
To determine the appropriate time interval for quantum annealing, a theoretical model is presented that considers both the TQI and quench dynamics simultaneously.
By applying this model to an exact cover problem representing a key class of NP-complete problems, the algorithm's success and failure times can be calculated in quench units of time.
As anticipated, the optimal annealing time follows an inverse relationship with the quantum speed.
Moreover, the results indicate that significant deviations from this simple relationship arise when quantum fluctuations interact strongly with local classical forces.

In the industries of manufacturing, automation, and robotics, exceptions and unexpected events are frequently encountered during business processes. Although academic research conformance checking methods are effective for detecting deviations, they are difficult to apply due to limited consideration of simultaneous occurrences in processes. This paper addresses this limitation by exploring an alternative approach to handling process data, focusing on initial segments of executed instances. We first review established definitions of infix alignments and their role in determining deviations, then discuss challenges associated with existing conformance checking methods, before proposing research directions to advance conformance verification using infix alignments in manufacturing and automation industries.

Researchers investigated screening and coilability in infinite-layer nickelate LiNiO2 using a Hubbard model within a two-band, two-flavor framework that accounts for both the main and remote band states. They discovered that including the remote $e_g$ states significantly enhances both screening and coilability due to the additional available states which can be accessed by a spin flip. This increase effectively reduces the effective charge and improves the on-site Coulomb interaction. A larger effective interaction promotes charge localization and hinders charge carrier movement between the main and remote states; as a result, the system of coupled states becomes equivalent to a single-state system with increased interaction. The system's Mott transition is driven by charge localization, and since the system is spin-degenerate (due to the combined main and remote states), it will be ferromagnetic or exhibit some form of long-range order. Furthermore, ferromagnetism or another type of ordered state may emerge due to the exchange interaction mediated by these states and could potentially give rise to magnetic or ordered insulators with charge and/or lattice symmetry. Notably, doped LiNiO2 exhibits metallic behavior, suggesting it contains a primary $t_{2g}$ hole that resides in the lower $t_{2g}$ state and is heavily screened by the $e_g$ states, resulting in strong coilability for these states and suggesting it could exhibit long-range ordered behavior under appropriate conditions.

This research examines the long-term behavior of phase mixing and dispersion in the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation, focusing on how the limit as the product of the collision cross-section $\sigma$ and frequency factor $\omega$ approaches zero affects the Boltzmann equation's behavior and leads to the Landau equation, particularly in large-scale settings and under specific initial conditions. We demonstrate that without the confinement of periodic boundaries, the Boltzmann operator's strong dissipation rapidly causes any initial density to blend into a Gaussian distribution with the velocity of particles in the limit. We further show that this dynamic, when combined with a weak singularity near velocity zero, rapidly transforms the equation into its modified version and, with initial velocities decaying quickly, the long-term behavior of the velocity component decays similarly to that of the scalar case, with a rate of $\t ^{-5/2}$.

We used IASI satellite images to reanalyze sea surface imagery that Cox and Munk used to study wave slopes. Our reexamination of their work utilized more precise data, reevaluating their key findings and mathematical models. In addition, we compared sea surface imagery with measurements from a radar and wave buoy, as well as data from IASI, taking into consideration the accuracy of each measurement method. Our study also explored the use of infrared data for measuring sea surface roughness, with potential applications for estimating changes in air-sea friction caused by weather patterns on a global scale.

When designing a software system, the goal is to minimize the cost of making it fail. A method is proposed to select an efficient and non-redundant set of test cases to optimize system cost. This involves using data from past tests and applying the singular value decomposition to identify the underlying test case characteristics. By solving the corresponding equation with a minimum gauge condition, an optimal sequence of test cases is determined. This process can be accelerated by implementing a parallel version of the algorithm using a shared memory model and the OpenMP technology, significantly reducing computation time when working with a large number of test cases.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. Within social media, users' opinions on the pandemic are freely expressed, often revealing both fear and humor. However, these sentiments can also spread hatred and fear, making it essential to monitor public sentiment during the pandemic. This paper analyzes Chinese Weibo data from March to May 2020, focusing on mentions of the pandemic to evaluate public sentiment through various extraction methods and classification models. Using manually labeled baseline samples, we accurately classify the remaining dataset with 96.30% accuracy using an ensemble model combining BERT, BidiAF, and AFDI, along with an automated labeling system.

Initially, the Bloch-Grosscka model was adapted for cuprate superconductors by adding an interlayer coupling, and a London moment was introduced to the interplane Bloch electrons. Although the model was able to reproduce the key temperature-dependent features of the cuprates, generalizing it to incorporate the charge density oscillations observed in experiments was challenging. A simplified approach was devised to achieve this generalization by considering the interplay between the intra- and interlayer electrons within a modulated potential, which could be altered by a London moment. Although this simplified model did not fully replicate all the experimental data, it was shown that the model's accuracy could be improved by including additional factors such as the phase of the charge density wave and the intensity of the local potential.

In the dense matter found within neutron stars, the sound speed at the density of nuclear matter indicates valuable information about the matter's equation of state.
